speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over our Thanksgiving weekend, the eyes of the world were focused on Reykjavik. There, the Leaders of the United States and the Soviet Union met to reinvigorate the summit process begun last year in Geneva and to narrow some of the many differences which divide them. Their goal was to give the process impetus, and they succeeded.
Arms control and security are the central international issues of our time and the manner of their resolution will shape the global outlook for decades to come.
It is still too early to provide a final assessment of this latest meeting. The task now in Washington and in Moscow is to ensure that the progress which appears to have been made is not wasted. All Governments share in this responsibility and we in Canada must do our part.
Today, as a contribution to our own discussion and debate within this House, and in the country at large, I would like to make some brief observations about the nature of the Reykjavik meeting in the broad context of East-West relations.

First, Sir, it would be well to remember that Reykjavik was but one staging point in the difficult and unending process of managing the relations between East and West. During the meeting, both sides moved more than anyone had thought possible. Immediately after the meeting, both sides reflected their disappointment that the breakthrough that was so close did not occur. Now, reflecting on that progress, both sides agree that the proposals made in Iceland are still on the table, still in negotiation.
This process of building East-West relations has been proceeding with renewed intensity since January, 1985. Reykjavik was designed not to conclude new agreements but to lay the ground for them. Whether history will judge it a success depends entirely on the use that is made of the progress in Iceland.
The most notable aspect of the Reykjavik meeting is the extent to which both sides were able to reach understandings
on the whole range of nuclear weapons and testing. They agreed provisionally to reduce by 50 per cent within five years the main components of their strategic nuclear arsenals: land-based missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and strategic bombers. At one point in their discussion, they also agreed to eliminate ballistic missiles completely in 10 years.
On intermediate-range nuclear weapons, there was similar provisional agreement on their complete elimination from Europe within five years, with the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. each retaining only 100 warheads in Soviet Asia and the continential U.S.A. respectively. The U.S.A. and the Soviet Union also agreed on the need to negotiate reductions in short-range nuclear arsenals.
There was mutual acceptance of a step-by-step process for reducing nuclear tests, leading eventually to a complete cessation of tests once nuclear weapons had been abolished. There was a broad convergence of views on the verification procedures to be applied to the various measures.
The fact that such detailed discussions occurred and resulted in such wide-ranging, if tentative, agreement attests to the seriousness and dedication with which the two sides have been approaching their task. The main significance lies in the demonstration that major, negotiated reductions in nuclear arsenals need not be an impossible dream.
At Reykjavik three lessons were reinforced. The first two are: both sides are serious; and arms control is possible. But the third lesson is that arms control will not come easily. It is a deliberate and difficult process.
The more sobering element of reality as it has emerged from Reykjavik lies in the fact that the two sides remain far apart in their views on the future role of strategic defences. This is not a question of saying yes or no to SDI but of finding a way of managing the research on defensive weapons in which both sides are engaged.
A key issue between the two Governments is whether research is limited to the laboratory under the existing ABM Treaty. That, Sir, is a treaty with two signing parties: the United States and the Soviet Union. Its text does not refer directly to research, although the private negotiating record of either side may mention research. The agreement on what precisely is intended in that treaty is for these two Governments which are the parties to the agreement to work out.
It is important to note that this is a different issue from the debate we have seen in recent months over what is allowed by agreed statement "D" of the ABM treaty referring to ABM systems based on other physical principles. Our interest in

Canada is to ensure strict adherence to that treaty, and continued respect by both sides for the integrity of this fundamental arms control document.
The situation today in no way represents a step backward from the situation as it existed prior to the Reykjavik meeting. Technological, political and legal uncertainties and disagreements have always characterized the debate on strategic defence. Even in this area, however, there has in our judgment been some movement toward better mutual understanding, in that the legitimacy of research related to strategic defence is now accepted by both sides. In a treaty that refers explicitly only to "development, testing and deployment", the issue has become, in effect, what are the limits of permissible research.

Mr. Speaker, we ought not to allow ourselves to focus exclusively on nuclear and strategic arms questions as if they constituted the totality of East-West relations. True, these issues have inescapably become the central element of this relationship, but they should not be seen in isolation from the broader context. There are other areas of arms control, most notably in relation to chemical weapons, where there is ground for cautious optimism. Further, we understand that on human rights questions and on a range of bilateral matters, progress continues to be made.
Mr. Speaker, I should add that I was encouraged by my own talks on human Rights with Soviet Foreign Minister Shevardnadze, when he visited Ottawa. Our discussion was frank and more open than I believe has been the case before. Canada believes progress here and on regional issues is essential to enable us to establish trust in each other's intentions. This process of building trust is far from finished.
Peace and security require patience and persistence. Emotional swings between exaggerated expectations and gloomy foreboding do not facilitate the necessarily careful and painstaking way in which difficult policy choices must be tackled.
As both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and 1 have made clear, the USA and USSR have made remarkable progress on the central arms control and disarmament issues over the past months. They are still seriously engaged in the task of seeking compromise on remaining areas of disagreement.
[DOT] (UIO)
We are encouraged by the public undertakings of both the President and the General Secretary to build on the progress which was achieved at Reykjavik. The resumption last Wednesday in Geneva of the nuclear and space negotiations can only be regarded as more good news.

The superpowers have succeeded in bringing a major arms control agreement tantalizingly close.
We cannot stop here. We have to move ahead. Arms control is a fragile process. Its environment must be protected. It is
therefore doubly important that all actions be resisted which might be seen as weakening or unravelling the existing international framework on which East-West relations and arms control are built.
Much attention has been focused on SDI and the ABM Treaty. The Geneva negotiations will need to resolve the differences that continue to exist here. Progress in other areas should not be held hostage to the resolution of these difficulties. Our European allies are especially concerned with intermediate nuclear forces. Canada would like to see an agreement in this area as well as in the area of strategic weapons, which threaten us directly.
Canada believes firmly in the value of the confidential negotiating forum. It is, in the end, irreplaceable. But it can be aided through techniques such as special envoys and, as we have just seen, by summits. We would urge both superpowers to continue to use all these techniques, and not rely on negotiating in public.
If a summit in Washington this fall is now unlikely, setting a date for early next year could help maintain the impetus of the process.
Canada is involved in East-West relations as a member of the NATO alliance. That alliance is the foundation of our security. What happens at the negotiating table between the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. has a direct bearing on our own security. We are at the same time a nation dedicated to peace. Canadians have always worked for peace and international understanding. We have not, and will not, hesitate to make our views known: Publicly when that is appropriate; privately on a permanent basis.
But Canada's role is not simply to give advice. Many of the persisting obstacles to negotiating progress arise directly from a lack of trust. The priority attention Canada has given to verification issues in particular attacks this question directly. Arms control agreements alone do not produce security; confidence in compliance produces security. Verification justifies that confidence. Such an approach enhances the credibility of Canada's counsel.
Canada's participation as a western country in the process of building East-West relations will continue. The visit to Canada in the last month of Soviet Foreign Minister Shevardnadze and the Czechoslovak Prime Minister were part of this process. Early next month I will travel to Vienna for the opening of the CSCE follow-up meeting which deals with East-West relations from the human rights, security, economic and human contact dimensions. It provides us with yet another opportunity to move the process ahead in an integrated comprehensive manner.
Our hopes for real progress in East-West relations were strengthened by the developments at Reykjavik. Canada has been in touch with both sides, before and since the meeting in Iceland. We will continue to use all our resources to help the United States and the Soviet Union build on what they began.

Mr. Speaker, I should say at the outset that I have rather mixed feelings about the appearance here today of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the comments he has just made. I should also say at the outset that he had the courtesy to deliver to me a copy of his comments this morning so I have had an opportunity to look at them. I am pleased that he is here and using the House as a forum within which to advise the Canadian people and parliamentarians of the policy of the Government. However, I hope that when he appears before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade he will be somewhat more forthcoming and somewhat more courageous than he has been here today. It is not clear to me why this statement has been delivered in the House of Commons.

I must say I was very disappointed in the substance of what he just told us, Mr. Speaker. We have been offered nothing but generalities and cliches on disarmament and Canadian policy.

His comments are optimistic in the aftermath of the Reykjavik Summit meeting. He saw progress arising from that summit between Mr. Reagan and Mr. Gorbachev. To a degree I share that optimism. However, I must say it has been very much tempered by the outcome.

In my view, a historic opportunity was lost in Reykjavik. Will there be others? We can only hope so. Mr. Speaker, behind the clouds the sun continues to shine and for a few moments in Reykjavik, the clouds lifted.

Yet the clouds returned and, as I said, the opportunity was lost. It was lost because of the insistence of the United States on continuing to develop its star wars initiative, the Strategic Defence Initiative, beyond laboratory testing.
The Minister declared, and I read from his statement:
]Translation]
"Canadians have always worked for peace and international understanding. Wc have not hesitated, and will not hesitate to make our views known: Publicly when that is appropriate, privately on a permanent basis."
Canada has not made known its true views on the SDI initiative of the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs certainly did not do that this morning. In fact, if anything, the Minister's statement waffled on a very important issue. I am amazed at the extent to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has attempted not to speak out, having declared in the closing paragraphs of his remarks that Canada never hesitates to speak out.
Statements by Ministers
The Minister referred to the Limitation of Anti-Ballistic Missile Systems Agreement which was adopted in May, 1972, between the superpowers. That ABM Treaty is very much at the heart, from a legal point of view, of the disputes surrounding the Strategic Defence Initiative. With respect to it the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
The agreement on what precisely is intended in that treaty is for these two Governments who are the parties to the agreement to work out.
That sounds as though this were some sort of private contractual relationship between two individuals or two corporations. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself has said, this treaty goes to the very heart of world security, yet he refuses to offer the Government's view as to how the star wars initiative can be rationalized with the terms of that treaty.
I will read the most relevant article from the treaty. Article V reads:
1.	Each Party undertakes not to develop, test, or deploy ABM systems or components which are sea-based, air-based, space-based, or mobile land-based.
2.	Each Party undertakes not to develop, test, or deploy ABM launchers for launching more than one ABM interceptor missile at a time from each launcher, nor to modify deployed launchers to provide them with such a capability, nor to develop, test, or deploy automatic or semi-automatic or other similar systems for rapid reload of ABM launchers.
Does the Secretary of State for External Affairs not have a view on the application of Article V to the Strategic Defence Initiative of the United States? I suspect that he does have a view and has not yet disclosed it to us in the House. I hope he will before the committee.
My real point this morning is not to debate legalities, not to get into nitpicking legal argument as to whether something is or is not covered by Article V. The real issue is political will, the importance of world leaders exercising their respective judgments on behalf of the peoples they lead and not being the captives of nitpicking bureaucrats. That applies to the Soviet Union as it applies to the United States and the Minister. If I ever saw a statement which was prepared by nitpicking bureaucrats, it is the one which the Minister read to us this morning. When Pierre Elliott Trudeau put the nuclear accountants in their place he made the point that it is up to leaders to exercise their judgment. That is the only way in which progress is going to be made. That is the way in which progress must be made. There must be trust between the leaders.
I suggest to the Minister and my colleagues in the House that the Strategic Defence Initiative is, by definition, a statement of mistrust. We in our Party see it as much more than a statement of mistrust. We see it as destabilizing, as an escalation in the arms race and as an incredible waste of precious resources which could and should be applied to raising the quality of life on this planet, especially in the Third World. We all know that in the long term it is that growing economic disparity which poses the greatest threat to mankind.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has not spoken out. He has not revealed his true beliefs. Surely he saw

Reykjavik as a unique opportunity for a major breakthrough in arms control and disarmament, and that major opportunity has been jeopardized. I know that as the Minister watched this scenario unfold he probably recalled the words of Shakespeare who said:
There is a tide in the affairs of men,
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
I ask the Minister to do his part, to speak out to the United States, the Soviet Union and the world to ensure that that tide is recaptured in the interest of international peace and security.

Mr. Speaker, I will begin my comments by agreeing with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that the whole world was indeed watching what was taking place at Reykjavik on Thanksgiving weekend. It watched with a great deal of hope that the two superpowers might reach an agreement, not simply on limiting weapons of one kind or another but on serious reductions of weapons. That was the hope, not only of Canadians but of people throughout the planet.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the superpowers have made progress. That is true. The Minister stressed that the two parties have agreed to put certain suggestions they discussed in Reykjavik on the table. They intend to continue their discussions, and I agree. We have seen progress at certain levels, but it is also true that the superpowers have lost an historic opportunity. I hope that this time, the loss will be only temporary, but the fact is there just the same.

They did lose what was almost within their grasp. It is with some sadness that the people of Canada and all the people of the world note this reality.
In this context we in this House have been rightly critical of the Soviet Union for many years, not only on internal arrangements about civil liberties, on which there is total agreement in this House, but in particular of the Soviet Union's reluctance to open itself to outside observers to ensure that agreements entered into were implemented. As I said, we have been rightly critical. Those of us who live in open societies have been trying to feel our way toward sensible proposals which could lead, not only to arms control but to disarmament. We have been critical of the Soviet's reluctance to open up.
A year ago last summer in Geneva I had occasion to have very serious discussions, back to back, with the principal Soviet negotiator Mr. Karpov on the one hand, and the principal American negotiator, Max Kampelman, on the other. Let me say, in the context of what took place at Reykjavik, that having had these conversations with these two key representatives of the two superpowers I certainly did not come away
with any high degree of optimism. It seemed to me a year ago last summer that both the Soviet Union and the United States were locked into positions that made it almost impossible for an agreement to be reached. Neither side seemed willing to make key concessions.
I wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs had been open on this point.
If one looks at what was agreed to at Reykjavik in terms of the shifting of positions, I think it is clear that the Soviet Union made the major moves. There were half a dozen key positions, including verification procedures, to which they rigidly held. We saw them shift ground as they needed to shift ground. It seems to me that when we in the House and throughout western democratic society see that kind of move taking place, particularly under new leadership in the Soviet Union, which may now be challenged as a result of some shifts that have been taken, we ought to give credit where credit is due. I see the Secretary of State nodding his head in agreement with that point.
There were moves on both sides, but the major moves were taken by the Soviet Union. I think we must carefully look for the stumbling block that led to the breakdown of what could have been an historic agreement. I believe the evidence is very clear, if we do not blind ourselves to it. The stumbling block, as I see it and which, frankly, as disinterested observers in Europe and indeed the United States and our country see it, was in fact President Reagan's insistence on the United States' right to go ahead with the development of testing of star wars during the next 10 years and the right to deploy such a system at the end of the decade. I use those words with care and say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that such development, testing and deployment are in clear violation of Article V of the ABM Treaty.
I would have liked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to say that clearly in the House today. It is very important for us to understand as a nation, and very important for the world to understand that the stumbling block to reaching an agreement in terms of all the documents that have emerged and statements that have been made has been the United States' insistence in these discussions on its right to break the existing ABM Treaty. I believe that is the unvarnished reality.
The spokesperson for the Liberal Party has read Article V so I will not repeat it. However, not only is the U.S. proposal a violation of Article V, it is important to note that by pursuing this course of action at Reykjavik the United States in fact reversed Secretary of State Shultz's commitment to a "restrictive interpretation" of the treaty which is very precise in prohibiting testing and development of the star wars system.
In this context let me say that the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself cited Mr. Shultz on this point in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on December 4, 1985. He cited with approval Mr. Shultz's restrictive interpretation definition of the ABM

Treaty. Furthermore, not only did our External Affairs Minister correctly stress the restrictive interpretation and correctly point out that Mr. Shultz, in disagreement with some other U.S. officials, had taken this restrictive interpretation, since the two key members of the U.S. delegation who in fact negotiated the ABM Treaty have confirmed that the intent and wording of the ABM Treaty was to exclude the development and testing of systems like star wars. Mr. Gerard Smith and Mr. John Rhinelander, two principals of the team that the Americans had negotiating the ABM Treaty, are saying that that treaty prohibits quite categorically the development and testing of a star wars type system. That is precisely what President Reagan was insisting upon as the United States, right at Reykjavik.
In today's statement the Secretary of State for External Affairs made no reference whatsoever to this crucial point, which is the nub of the issue. Why is the Secretary of State for External Affairs avoiding the central question? It is one matter to go and talk about the precise limits of research, but it is quite another to miss the key point, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has done.
Not many weeks ago he was quite happy to talk in specific reference to the ABM Treaty and a restrictive definition. Now he has shifted ground entirely and says that what is at issue and what must be talked about, according to the Secretary of State, are: "the limits on permissible research which now has become the issue". Surely such a narrow discussion as "the limits on permissible research" is now described as the issue only because the United States administration has refused to back away from insisting on its right to test and deploy the star wars system. Instead of forthrightly criticizing the Reagan administration for this, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is now helping them get the focus away from their desire to violate the ABM Treaty. I say to the Minister that this is unacceptable to the people of Canada and unacceptable to all those who want independent nations to work toward disarmament at this point in world history.
Surely Canada must show some real independence in this matter. We must be telling the Reagan administration that it is wrong. The Secretary of State for External Affairs says: "It is not a question of saying yes or no to SDI but of finding a way of managing the research on defensive systems in which both sides are engaged". With respect, I say to the Minister that he is wrong. It is a matter of saying no to SDI, whether it is developed in the Soviet Union or the United States. The ABM Treaty was quite specifically designed to avoid the development of new technologies for this kind of weapons system. It is time that we put an end to this kind of lunacy in the world and we have an oblilgation to say so.
What seems to be clearly involved in the pursuit of the Reagan administration-not the American people-is the scuttling of the ABM Treaty. The Minister talked about looking at these new grounds for discussion and new grounds for agreement. I ask him, what use can a new agreement be if

we stand by and watch either one of the superpowers undermine existing agreements? We have now a rather fragile instrument in the world in this field and that is the ABM Treaty. We have an obligation as a nation not to stand back and let the superpowers do whatever they will. We must exercise our influence with dispassion, with care and with intelligence, and that means when one of them is clearly wrong we should say they are wrong. When one of them is taking steps which could seriously jeopardize the development of peace, we should be saying so.
I want to say in this context that the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau-despite all those other particular matters about which my Party and I disagreed with him-had an appropriate sense of the role that Canada could play. He, along with Olaf Palme, the Prime Minister of India and the President of Mexico, had shown remarkable independence in criticizing both the United States and the Soviet Union when they were wrong. I wish we had that kind of independent thought functioning in foreign policy, especially on disarmament, today.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to think carefully about what he has said, note that he missed the essence of the problem, reconsider his policy and start showing some independence which could have some concrete results leading to disarmament in this world of ours.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill to amend the National Anthem Act remedies a situation which has existed in the words of our National Anthem "O Canada" since it was first approved by the Parliament of Canada, particularly the reference to "all our sons" which leaves out a very important sex in our society. This amendment would eliminate those words "all our sons" and replace them with the words "all of us", thereby eliminating the sexist reference in our National Anthem.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill enacts a new statute called the Crime Victims Assistance Act. Those who are familiar with the administration of justice in Canada will know that there is no recognition or status given in our system to the victims of crime. This legislation will remedy that situation and provide specific remedies for victims of crime. It is the kind of legislation which is long overdue.
It was referred in the last session of the House of Commons to the Committee on Justice for consideration.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the Hon. Member have leave to introduce the Bill?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, the objective of this proposed legislation is to protect the privacy and freedom of the individual. Increasingly, the Social Insurance number has been employed as a kind of national identifier. It has been used by landlords, merchants, banks, credit agencies and insurance companies in a way which involves the potential invasion of the privacy of the individual, opening up to institutions and agencies information which should not be publicly available.
The intent of this Bill is to restrict the requirement of the Social Insurance Number only to those activities that are covered by Acts of Parliament and require the use of that number, which was the original intent of the SIN. My Bill would restore that practice.

Mr. Speaker, in the last 48 hours 1 have had the opportunity to spend several periods of time talking with various agricultural organizations and groups in western Canada. It is hard to put into words the depth of concern and anxiety that they feel about the incredible crisis being felt in our commodity markets. Western Canada and, indeed, the entire agricultural sector of Canada know that they are in the fight of their lives, that many signs and portents are clearly apparent which point to a challenge and a threat to the basic underlying strength of this sector. I say this because of the actions by other countries to substantially increase the support and assistance they give to agricultural export markets.
The problem we face is one of basic over-supply of many of our basic commodities, particularly in the area of grain. We all know exactly how serious that is and how, at the present time, there is no apparent answer. I grant full well that the decision taken at the meetings in Uruguay to commence negotiations was a step in the right direction. However, it is a step that will take years to bring to fruition. In the meantime we are faced with the actions in the United States under the U.S. Farm Bill, which are not over. Those who think that the worst impacts of

the U.S. Bill have been felt up until now are kidding themselves. It is clear that the discretion under that piece of U.S. legislation to continue to ratchet down prices and provide export subsidies will continue. The discussions I had with U.S. officials in Punta del Este, Uruguay, only confirmed that.
It is clear that the objective is basically to put a lot of us in the agricultural trade out of business. The high volume-low price theory is being emphasized. No mercy will be shown to any country. This clearly points out the necessity for an export strategy, a world-wide trade strategy specifically designated to assist our agricultural sector. We do not have this at the present time. There is no trade strategy on agriculture. There is but a series of ad hoc, capricious reactions to events. There has been a wide variety of attempted bail-outs, but there is nothing coherent, nothing that is able to provide any clear direction as to how we might meet the challenge we face.
I would like to give Hon. Members an example of this. At the negotiations undertaken in Uruguay to put agriculture on the table it was clear that many countries felt that Canada was not playing its role to the fullest, in essence, not pulling its fair share. I say this because one of the things we obviously avoided doing at those meetings was make any effort to introduce into the talks how we could substantially increase the earnings and incomes of many Third World countries which, as a group, have come to form our second-largest customer over the years.
The level of Canadian agricultural exports to Third World countries over the last five years has dropped by almost 40 per cent. No one can take satisfaction in that figure. One would think that it would be in the Canadian interest to put into place the type of measures or proposals which would give much stronger levels of assistance to those countries in order to increase their cash flows so that they might be able, once again, to come back in to the market and procure our various commodities. However, Canada took no such initiatives in that direction. I report to Members of the House that this inaction caused a great deal of regret on the part of many officials of other countries to whom I spoke who asked, "What is wrong with Canada?" I was asked why we were not out there leading in this particular area.
I see that the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) is in the House. I would like to repeat to him what his colleague from Argentina had to say about the performance at Cairns. It was not particularly complimentary. In other words, Canada did not achieve the type of stimulation in terms of a broad-based discussion of the areas we had to initiate.
Oh, oh!

Madam Speaker, Members opposite laugh. Out of deference to the sensitivities of the Minister I will not repeat the words that were used and printed in The Financial Post and other newspapers for all to see.
The fact of the matter is we do not have a clear strategy as to what we are attempting to achieve. To make matters worse,

Canagrex
we now have legislation before us to dissolve Canagrex after some two years. Once again the Government has shown its dispatch in terms of dealing with these types of matters. The formation of Canagrex was designed to give Canada the opportunity to develop new markets around the world for a wide variety of agricultural products that are not covered by the Canadian Wheat Board. In a sense, Canagrex was the equivalent of the Canadian Wheat Board. It dealt with a range of alternate commodities. I only wish to point out what is apparent, that is, the illogic and inconsistency of Conservative Members of Parliament from western Canada who on any and almost all occasions stand up and swear by the sanctity of the Canadian Wheat Board, but who are not prepared to grant the same type of resources to other agricultural commodities. How is it logical to say that what is good for grains is not good for fruits, vegetables, honey and other products?
Because farm groups don't want it.

I hear a tinny voice from the background. Of course the farmers want it. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture supported it. Is that not a farm group? The last I heard, it represented a lot of farmers.
I suppose the Conservative Party no longer recognizes the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Tory Members have dismissed it. I want it put on the record that members of the Conservative Party no longer recognize the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. That will come as some news to the Federation. Now we know one of the reasons why the Government is getting rid of Canagrex. It refuses to recognize a large part of the Canadian agricultural sector. It says it does not exist. It is invisible to the eyes of Tory Members. Now I begin to understand. It is simply this kind of blindness on the part of Conservative Members that prevents us from keeping Canagrex.
What was Canagrex designed to do? Who is going to quarrel with me when I say that it was designed to do market development? A primary and essential requirement is to open up new markets for agricultural commodities. Anyone who is involved in international trade will say that it takes time and resources to develop a market. It is not developed overnight. There has to be investment, there has to be a cultivation of networks and there has to be promotion. It may take three or four years before sales begin and, as we well know, many producers do not have those kinds of resources. They do not have the staying power to go into a market and use their front-end investments to allow them over a period of years to develop the capacity to sell. Yet that is the only way to do it. Canagrex was designed to do that initial market promotion and development and to give it a chance to stick.
What was wrong with having an organization representing a number of commodity sectors doing market development and promotion on behalf of all commodity sectors and opening up those opportunities? We hear such brave words about the need to open up access to markets. As we all know, the Conservative
Party virtually restricts itself to the United States of America. That is the only place about which it is concerned. For many of the other countries of the world where there is demand for our products it is not prepared to invest the time or money or to put the organizational skill to work to make that happen.
I can give you an example of this, Madam Speaker. Three or four years ago I went on a tour of refugee camps in Central America. I found to my delight that one of the major products we sold to that area was beans from Manitoba, a potential alternate crop that will pick up the slack that will occur as our grain markets are faced with a squeeze-play between the United States and the European Economic Community. There is an incredible opportunity to open up those markets in many of those countries. Again, those markets in Central America were opened up through very careful work which occurred over a long period of time. That example could be applied to a wide variety of nations throughout the world.
It is clear from all the testimony and evidence the committee heard that many Canadian farm groups and farm producers are not capable of mounting a long-term developmental investment. Therefore, we brought in Canagrex to make it happen, to allow those groups to find the markets and to invest in the promotion. That has now been taken away. Once again, these groups have been side-swiped by the great theology of the market-place: go forward on your own. However, that is not the way it works.
Certainly every other country including the great fountainhead of market-place theology, the United States, is making every effort to provide major support for various commodity sectors. We are not doing it, though. We are being too pristine and pure about it. God forbid that Canada should advance and expand its agricultural markets. That would run against the grand theology.
When looking at the figures, it is interesting to note how these markets have been shrinking in the last couple of years. Yet this brave new Government is eliminating one of the few major resources we had designed to offset that shrinkage. Furthermore, I think the Government can be properly accused of fooling and perhaps even misleading many of the farm organizations. The Government said it did not like Canagrex but that it would replace it with similar resources and similar efforts through other government organizations. It said that it did not want another Crown corporation because it already had enough, so it would use the Export Development Corporation and the trade offices of External Affairs. It said it would put new money in the Estimates of the External Affairs Trade Department in order to provide an effective alternative or replacement.
Where is that replacement? Can anyone find it? Is there anything in the Export Development Corporation that will provide an effective alternative to Canagrex? No. In fact, suggestions have been made by the press that the Tories want to get rid of the Export Development Corporation. They want to wipe it off the books and restrict its activities. Where is the new money for agriculture in the Estimates of the External
October 21, 1986

Affairs Department for development and promotion of trade? Once again, there is nothing but a blank page. There is no alternative being provided.
At a crucial period in the life of Canadian agriculture, a time when it is fighting for its life to maintain markets around the world and to acquire new ones, the Canadian Government has made a clear and unmistakable decision to pull the props out, to retreat, to withdraw and to recede from those markets. It is absolutely incomprehensible. It defies logic, common sense and intelligence.
At a time when we face this incredible problem around the world, when we face the attack of the U.S. Farm Bill, when we see the kind of export promotion the European Economic Community is doing and when we face incredible pressure on grain trade, knowing that we have to find and develop new markets, why is the Ministry in full retreat? It is in retreat simply for reasons of ideological purity or theological precision. No one can understand the kind of curious motivation which works inside the heads of Tories. However, we do know that Canadian farmers are being left stranded in the international market with no support, no resources and no capacity to compete.
One can only say that eventually Tories will pay the price. We know what is happening in the farm sectors across Canada now. We are aware of the kind of protests that are being raised and of the kind of anger that is being shown. We are aware of the frustration that exists.
This Government came in with a pocketful of promises. Every time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saw two farmers at a crossroads he had five more promises to make.
Three hundred and thirty-eight altogether.

Three hundred and thirty-eight promises, and the count is still rising. Everywhere there was a promise: "I will do more. I will provide more. I will pay more." But when you get down to the hard reality, it is retreat, withdrawal, elimination.
It is very clear that one of the important elements in developing new international markets is research and development, to develop new products and new strains of commodities. Yet, once again what do we have from the Conservative Government when it comes to agricultural research and development? We have cut back, elimination, close down, shut off. Once again, there is a total contradiction between promise and performance.
We feel it is important to bring to the attention of Canadians the reason we oppose this Bill. This Government is guilty of indifference to the important issue of how Canadian farmers are going to be able to survive and grow in a very tough and competitive international trading environment.

I was interested in the speech by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). He crystalized the whole down-grading which has taken place in agriculture commodities and sales.
If you look through the approximately 20 Tory promises in the 1984 election you will see that a lot of those promises have been broken. Try as you may, nowhere do you find in those Tory promises that they are going to destroy or take away Canagrex from the producers of the less volume commodities.
Clearly, when Canagrex was established there were a lot of commodity groups who looked for support and assistance from the Government. Now they are being dashed by this action to destroy Canagrex. If we look at the promises the Tories made in the 1984 election we see many things, but they certainly did not promise to take away Canagrex.
For instance, they promised to abandon Section 31 of the Income Tax Act to reflect the principles of equity. Even though that was referred to a standing committee, and that committee made a report, no action was taken in that regard. They promised to establish a board of authority to control tobacco production and prices. The passage of that legislation was expedited in one sitting of the House, but still the Government has not passed the necessary Order in Council. They promised to expand the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act into a national farm and forestry rehabilitation act. They have never carried out that promise.
It seems to me that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg Fort- Garry has provided an excellent documentation of how the Government makes promises, but does not keep them, and how the Government talks about increasing export sales. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Prince Albert in July of 1984 said he was going to make Canada a superpower in agriculture commodity sales around the world. We only have to look at what his friend the President of the United States has done, and how he has responded, to see that Canadian farmers have never been put in a worse financial position in their lives. Not since R.B. Bennett was the Prime Minister has the situation been worse than the situation we have today under the present Government. The Hon. Member has made some excellent points. I would just ask him to respond to the questions I have raised.

Madam Speaker, I will be more than happy to go through the Hon. Member's recitation. What he is pointing out very clearly is that the problems that we face do require some very skillful and important forms of government legislation and initiative. It is not sufficient to withdraw the assistance of Government itself. We know full well that the export market in agricultural commodities is one that is shifting quite substantially. The danger posed to many of our agricultural products, because of the Canada-U.S. trade negotiations, is also very serious. Yet what we see happening on the domestic side, in terms of preparation by investing

October 21, 1986
Canagrex
resources, investing in research, investing in a proper support system, investing in export assistance, is that none of that has taken place.
The proposals that we open up our access to markets seems to somehow preclude taking the appropriate action within our own domestic spirit. We are not helping to modernize the system, or provide for the innovation in the system, or the development of the markets in the system. That goes back to a fundamental flaw in the approach to trade, whether it is in agriculture or any other product. You cannot improve your capacity for trade unless you are also improving those products within your own domestic market-place, and the capacity to meet international demands and requirements.
Not only is it a question of promises not being fulfilled, but many of the important and constructive programs are being eliminated. How can a cut-back in agricultural research be justified? How can anyone in their right mind assume that we will be able to respond to new international competitive forces when we are cutting back on our research stations, or university programs on agricultural research? It simply begs logic and common sense to do that. Yet, that is what is going on. You only have to look at every resolution passed by every farm organization to say, "For God's sake, stop this insanity." At least in one area give us the capacity to keep our industry and commodities up to date and innovative. Nothing but a blind eye and a deaf ear has been turned to those pleas. As a result, we are substantially weakening the ability of our agricultural sector to compete and provide for the kind of forward-looking markets needed in the future.

speechtext: I would like to ask my colleague for Winnipeg-Fort Garry a question relating to the last point he made. Indeed, we are playing into the hands of the Americans somewhat in destroying Canagrex and reducing the competitiveness of Canadian farm producers by not having a government corporation doing the marketing for those farmers. How does he see this having an impact on our commercial relations with the Americans? Does he see this as a move on the part of the Government to destroy Canagrex so that they will kowtow to the Americans a little better and make friends? Then they indeed can get the free trade deal back on track, so the Americans feel happy about it? Does he feel that there is any relationship between the free trade negotiations and the fact that the Government has destroyed Canagrex?

It has been quite apparent in the statements made by the trade negotiator for the United States, as well as other officials in the United States, and Members of Congress, that they do not like the way we do business in Canada. They think we should be like them. As a result, one of the threats that we face in the Canada-U.S. negotiations is a clear challenge to things like our marketing board system, our supply management system and our transportation support programs. They are clearly part of what is being challenged.
I might refer the Hon. Member to a study done by the Canada West Foundation which came out just this month. It points out that a number of key agricultural sectors in western Canada, such as the feather trades, egg, poultry, turkey, and others, and the vegetable and horticultural trades would be wiped out at a moment's notice: they would not last 24 hours under Canada-U.S. negotiation.
It is very clear that what this Government is doing right across the board is tailoring many of its own domestic responses and programs to suit what it thinks is a compatible appearance and perception by the Americans. As a result the Americans do not like the idea that we would use the constructive ability of government to assist in these areas, whether it be by marketing boards or trading corporations to try to develop those areas. I think the Hon. Member has made an important point. We cannot ignore the clear relationship between the obsession regarding Canada-U.S. trade and the unwillingness to go forward to help our commodity producers to develop new markets through an operation like Canagrex.

Madam Speaker, I was afraid for a moment that you had not seen me.
1 would not want to miss this opportunity to contribute to the debate on the destruction of Canagrex by the Tories.
I would like to begin my remarks by congratulating you on your new position in the Chair which I have not yet had the opportunity to do. I know that you will discharge your functions with utmost non-partisanship. I am sure you will excel in that way and I want to take this opportunity to offer you my personal congratulations.
I am going to speak a little bit about this measure of the Conservative Government to dissolve Canagrex, although the words should really be to destroy Canagrex. Why are the Conservatives so bent on getting rid of this organization? Is it merely a partisan gesture on their part? You, being the nonpartisan person that you are, Madam Speaker, would know how partisan those Tories can be on occasion. But why destroy Canagrex? Why do it now?
Let me look into those two issues; first, the Bill. It is a very small piece of legislation with very few clauses. It has enormous ramifications as I see it on the agricultural industry of our country. The question that begs to be asked is, does this Bill have support in the farming community? It does not if we go back to the original group of people who supported the concept of having an international strategy through Canagrex in the first place. Let me list some of the people who advocated Canagrex and supported its establishment: the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Eastern Ontario Potato
October 21, 1986

Producers Council, the New Brunswick Potato Agency, the National Farmers Union; l'Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec; the Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board; the Canadian Pork Council; the Canadian Horticultural Council; the Ontario Flue Cured Tobacco Marketing Board; the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board and the Ontario Soybean Growers. I understand there were others who supported the original Bill to establish Canagrex provided that it had slight modifications. Those who supported that Bill were: the Canadian Food Processors Association; the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, the Alberta Swine Breeders, the Manitoba Cattle Producers; the Alberta Cattle Feeders; the PEI Potato Marketing Board; the Alberta Beekeeper's Association and the Western Stock Growers.
For whom does the Government pretend it is speaking in trying to dissolve the Canagrex Corporation?

Madam Speaker, perhaps the inherent contradiction in professing to be both progressive and conservative is becoming ever more obvious. In light of its policy aimed at dismantling Canagrex, it looks as though their Party should be labelled regressive conservative instead of progressive conservative. Is it one of the basic tenets of the Conservative Party that the state should not interfere like this with market forces? Is this the real identity of the Conservative Party? Did the Party's right extremists pressure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and lobby to have Canagrex put to rest? I wish Conservative Members opposite would enlighten us because it is crystal clear that the farming community does not support the abolition of Canagrex.
Madam Speaker, in my mail this morning I received an invitation from Le regroupement agro-alimentaire de Prescott-Russell, a groups of constituents who would like me to attend a seminar on the marketing of farm products. Here we have this Conservative Government bent on annihilating a Government agency designed to promote the marketing of agricultural products, yet a group of people from my own riding-which you know quite well, Madam Speaker, since you have to travel through it every time you leave your own riding to come here on Parliament Hill-has set up this seminar for November 29 this year. Here is what they are asking me: "Immediately reserve Saturday November 29 to come and promote the agricultural food industry in our counties. Saturday the 29th will be set aside to inform, educate, enlighten and brief all seminar participants on the possibility of processing and selling more farm products." As you can see, Madam Speaker, my constituents-like those in all other agricultural ridings throughout Canada, I am sure- want to boost the sale of their products precisely when the Conservative Party is trying to destroy Canagrex, our very own national marketing agency.

Why is it important to have Canagrex, Madam Speaker? Why is it important to keep it, particularly now? First, we
Canagrex
should look at the fact that the Progressive Conservative Party during the last election campaign promised the Canadian people that it would improve sales of agricultural products. I see a Conservative Member across the way from an agricultural area. I have something to read to him. I will read it slowly so that he can understand everything. The Conservative Party put out a press release dated July 5, 1984 entitled "Prince Albert Caucus Progressive Conservative Agenda for Government Policy Area: Agriculture". Here are some of the things the Tories said during the election campaign in that press release:
Canada can be a world superpower in agriculture. We have the land base, the climate, the technology and, most importantly, a strong and determined farm community.
Under Progressive Conservative Commitments, which is a euphemism for Tory promises we find:
We will work with all producers, whether they choose to establish a marketing board or another type of marketing sytem. Some commodities are sold and promoted by marketing boards and agencies; others are sold and promoted in different ways. A PC Government will respect any decision made by the producers.
I have just finished reading to you a list of producers who wanted to have a Canagrex agency, Madam Speaker.
I ask the Hon. Member, when he votes on this Bill will he respect the commitment made on July 5, 1984 by the Conservative Party? How will he reconcile his conscience with the way he votes? I suppose Tories can reconcile anything with their consciences. Fet me read further:
A PC Government will respect any decision made by the producers. Our goal is to assist farmers and, through such systems, to develop greater sales and a greater return for their various products.
What happened to that?
Fet me read further:
We have always recognized the valuable contribution of grain and oilseed exports to Canada's balance of payments. We will, therefore, work to increase exports and stimulate production to meet those export demands.
Another commitment:
A PC Government will develop a healthy Canadian agricultural industry by providing a strong agriculture research base through greater assistance for agricultural colleges, more funding for agricultural research and development and amending tax policy to encourage private sector investment.
I think all those promises I have read to you, Madam Speaker, have been broken in this Bill before us today. Every single one of them.
The next question is, why should we have a Canagrex, particularly now? The Member across the way who is heckling from behind the curtains should know that Canada is faced with a very grave situation in agriculture right now. This has been caused in large measure by an initiative outside of this country known as the U.S. Farm Bill. The official name is the Food Security Act of 1985 of the United States of America.
On what commodities?

That Bill applies to a large variety of commodities, to answer the Hon. Member. Although he heckles a

Canagrex
lot, he seems to be at least paying attention to my speech. The U.S. Farm Bill will affect everything from grain to milk to meat products, honey, and a variety of other commodities which will now be subsidized by the U.S. Government to a large and significant extent. The purpose is to displace foreign sales and replace them with U.S. sales. Some $70 billion U.S. will be injected into support programs to compete against Canadian products and others.
What are we doing as a country, as a Parliament, to ensure that we do not lose those sales? We are abolishing whatever small measures we have to help our agricultural industry. Some Tories across the way laugh at that. They are so partisan. Why can they not think for a minute about the agricultural community that sent them here? I guess they will have to reconcile that later, if not with their consciences at least with their voters. The agricultural community is not going to like this one bit.
I will take you on in any agricultural community anywhere in Canada.
The agricultural community of my riding is very upset with this Government, and rightfully so.
Look at their Member.
The agricultural community right across this country is displeased with the way this Conservative Government has failed to deliver on its promises.
What happened in Saskatchewan last night?

1 see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in the House. I will remind him that he said on February 4, 1985, in this House, as recorded in Hansard at p. 1963:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it very clear that this Government will very aggressively follow the export market for agricultural commodities.
And we have.

He continued:
Our Department has already entered into negotiations-
And we did.
-and had discussions and that role will be carried on more effectively-
And the results are showing.
-and more successfully with the Export Development Corporation properly financed.
We have done that. We have made those changes.

I ask the Minister what happened to that
commitment?
It is being fulfilled.
What happened to that commitment?
Look at the facts.

The Minister of Agriculture made those statements in this House on February 4, 1985, and in December of the same year the U.S. Farm Bill was passed with hardly any lobbying by Canadian authorities to ensure that it would not pass.
Nonsense.
I was in Washington; I spent three days looking at the U.S. Farm Bill.
Why did you not stay home? That is your problem.
I asked the people in Washington what kind of lobbying-
They told me not to send you down again.

-did the Government of Canada undertake in Washington to ensure that the U.S. Farm Bill would not pass? What was the name of the lobbying firm that was hired? After all, Canadians hired Michael Deaver for some other lobbying. I understand he lobbied very well but he was a rather controversial and expensive guy to have around.
They paid him pretty well.

For acid rain we had Michael Deaver. We have hired lobbyists in the past for other things. Yet, when it came time to lobby for Canadian farmers what happened? I asked our embassy in Washington who was the lobbyist, how much time was spent and how much money was paid? Do you know what they said? None, no lobbyist was hired. We have one person working in agriculture in Washington and she did some lobbying on her own. That is what we had to offer to Canadian farmers concerning a Bill involving $70 billion U.S. aimed directly at stealing our customers. We failed miserably, and what are we going to do now? We are going to compound the failure by abolishing our national agency-
No, we are just trying to eliminate one of your many failures.

-to provide the marketing. The Minister calls Canagrex a failure. That agency was supported by all the groups I mentioned, and I can repeat the list for the Minister's benefit, yet he calls it a failure. He has questioned the support of the agricultural community which I have just read for you, Madam Speaker. In so doing he is taking partisan shots, not at me but at all those agricultural organizations who wanted a Canagrex type of organization.

Have the courage to read the whole list.

Worst of all, he never even allowed the agency to work. Yet I am not convinced that he, although it is his Bill, was in favour of abolishing Canagrex.
Certainly was not.
Because I remember speeches he made in this House before the 1984 election when he liked the idea in the first place.
No one liked it.

The Member from the agricultural riding of Mississauga North says no one liked it. I invite him to read Hansard. It is excellent material and he should try reading some of the speeches of the now Minister of Agriculture in his days in opposition.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), when he delivered his November 8, 1984, economic statement, chose randomly to abolish a number of things and left his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, to carry the can. That is when he cancelled a number of agricultural research projects, Canagrex, and a whole list of other good measures which the Minister had previously supported. The Minister of Agriculture was forced to carry the can, but he should not. He should not be here to apologize for the Minister of Finance. He should let him make his own mistakes. He should tell the Minister of Finance to introduce his own dissolution Bills. The Minister of Agriculture should have told the Minister of Finance that he would not put up with this, that the Minister must reinstate Canagrex or he would move back to the back benches and do his job there for the farmers of Canada. That is what he should have done. But instead he took the easy, partisan role. He sat in his place and defended actions which he did not believe in.
As I said before, I believe that this move is wrong, particularly at this time when there are international pressures on our agricultural commodities. Let us reinstate Canagrex, give it back personnel and make it work for the benefit of Canadian farmers.

Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that he is the fifth Member from his Party to speak on this legislation. It has been made quite clear to us in this House that the Hon. Member and his Party oppose the legislation to wind up Canagrex. Is the Hon. Member aware that by continuing to put up speakers on this Bill he is delaying the opportunity of the House to deal with another very important piece of legislation relating to farmers, that is Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act which will provide Canadian farmers with more money now when there is such great concern for Canadian farmers?
Shame, shame!

The Hon. Member indicated that he supports Canadian agriculture. Would it not make a lot of sense for him
Canagrex
and his Party to wind up their discussion on this Bill and to move quickly to Bill C-12 in order to show that the Hon. Member and the Liberal Party support the provision of more money for farmers at this critical time in the life of Canadian agriculture?

Madam Speaker, that is an excellent question. It is not very well thought out, but it is excellent nevertheless-probably by accident. I have consulted with my colleague, the official critic, and we are perfectly willing to give unanimous consent to move to the other Bill. We could give it passage within 15 or 20 minutes and then revert to the Canagrex Bill, if that is the wish of Members across the way. I am sure we could get consent of all Parties in order to do that.
You had better check with your House Leader if you have one today.

I thank the Hon. Member from the vastly rural riding of York East for bringing this to my attention.
With regard to the fact that I am the fifth speaker on this issue, I have no moral lessons to take from Tories who delayed this House for one month for no reason other than to get Dalton Camp to write better speeches for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The only reason these Bills are taking longer to deal with is that the Government failed so miserably to bring the House back at the proper time. I am the deputy critic on agriculture for my Party. I represent 2,500 farmers and I am going to speak for them in this House, whether or not the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) or anyone else likes it.
Well, I sure don't like it.
Madam Speaker, I apologize to the Member for coming in a few minutes late. I missed part of his speech.
You're lucky, Dave.
What a shame that was.
Could the Member help me by indicating which agricultural organizations support his proposal?

That is an excellent question, Madam Speaker. I regret that he was not able, by his own admission, to listen to my entire speech. I could speak longer with the unanimous consent of the House.
I will review for the Member the organizations which had offered their support for the original Bill and those which had offered their support on the condition that slight modifications be made. The Member will understand that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is an umbrella group which represents 200,000 producers. It had offered its support on behalf of the agencies and organizations it represents. Other organizations which offered their total support to this Bill are the Eastern Canada Potato Producers Council, the New Brunswick Potato Agency, the National Farmers Union, the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, the Ontario Bean

Canagrex
Producers Marketing Board, the Canadian Pork Council, the Canadian Horticultural Council, the Ontario Flue Cured Tobacco Marketing Board, the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board and the Ontario Soybean Growers.
Associations, which supported the Bill providing minor modifications were made, include the Canadian Food Processors Association, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, the Alberta Swine Breeders, the Manitoba Cattle Producers, the Alberta Cattle Feeders, the P.E.I. Potato Marketing Board, the Alberta Beekeepers Association and the Western Stock Growers.
In direct response to the Member's question, not only large private corporations supported the deal, it was also supported by such groups as the Union des Producteurs Agricoles du Quebec which represents practically every farmer in that province. Madam Speaker, it is imperative that that which is absolutely and totally false not be allowed to stand in the House of Commons. The Western Stock Growers Association adamantly opposed Canagrex, as does the Alberta Swine Growers Association. For political reasons the Member chooses to put on the record the initial reaction when the Bill was announced. They sent delegations to Ottawa to tell Canadian parliamentarians to oppose that Bill. What he refers to as insignificant and modest changes were changes in the buy-sell clause which was offensive and wrong and put the independence of Canadian agriculture under government control in Ottawa. He may call that small, but that is why the Canadian farm community reacted with the distaste and disgust with which it did. It is unfortunate that a Member would put on the record of the House of Commons things which he knows are absolutely false.

Madam Speaker, had the Member listened instead of heckling, as he did for most of the time that I was speaking, he would have heard me list those organizations which indicated support at the time the original Bill was presented. If he spent more time listening and less time talking in this House he would have heard that. I invite him to review Hansard tomorrow and apologize later.

Madam Speaker, I am interested in the comments of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria). I think there is a deliberate move by the Government to do everything it can to hurt the agriculture industry. We need only look at the S23 million cut in the budget for agriculture research this year. It is clear that the Minister had the ground cut out from under him by the Prime Minister's office and the office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on black Thursday, November 8, 1984. It was a decision by the Department of Finance and the Prime Minister's Office.
In his testimony before the Agriculture Committee, the Minister of Finance apologized for this decision being taken by the Government. He also phoned the President of Canagrex, Mr. Ed Story. Obviously, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) is screaming his view because the Tory caucus was very divided on this issue and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was in opposition-
