speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me congratulate you on your new position. I look forward to working with you in the House and I know you will do an excellent job.
Many things have been said this morning that I believe cannot go unchallenged. In many ways it is unfortunate that the Opposition chooses such a tone in this debate because, while there are problems in Canadian agriculture as everyone knows, I believe that any fair minded person would have to admit that the Government is making an effort to address those problems. I can give specific details of those efforts if the occasion rises.
However, when one hears the Opposition come on as strongly as it does, and indicate that nothing is being done in light of some very significant problems, surely it is not doing a service to Canadian farmers, to the House or to anyone who takes pride in being associated with this institution. I say that more in sorrow than in anger.
Let me suggest to Hon. Members opposite that they would serve the people whom they represent and would serve the House much better in debate if they were to talk about some of the things that the Government has done. While they may be critical of the Government, they should at least recognize some of our accomplishments.
For example, they can talk about what we are doing for our export markets internationally. Last year, there was good news as far as the export of Canadian agricultural products was concerned. Members of the Official Opposition should know that last year Canada's share of wheat exports actually rose.
That was before the U.S. Farm Bill.

The Hon. Member should listen and put into practice some of the suggestions he makes for our side. That is after the U.S. BICEP Program and the Farm Bill had been in effect for about a year. We told the Americans when they were contemplating the U.S. Farm Bill that we did not think it would work, because a farmer's normal reaction to lower prices is to increase production and maintain revenue by having more volume at lower total revenue. That has in fact been borne out, because last year Canada's share of total wheat exports went up while the American share went down.
October 21, 1986

Any farmer in western Canada will say that they went into the crop year at the beginning of August with the lowest on-farm carry-over on record. It was approximately 800,000 tonnes, which is significant. No one in the Opposition pays any attention to that.
Let me put this in greater perspective. We faced the same situation in the early 1970s when there was a rather large surplus of grain around the world which was depressing the market. It is very similar to what is happening today, but our attitude today is that we will not let our farmers down. We will sell their grain and not see granaries full of unsold grain-even at low prices. We are much better off to sell at a lower price and keep the volume up than we are to do what the former Government did in the 1970s, which was to introduce a LIFT Program. I have the figures in front of me. Our exports went down from 18 million tonnes in 1969-70 to nine million tonnes in 1970-71. That was a direct result of a previous Liberal Government reacting to the farm community and not selling. We are not doing that. We are selling at record volumes.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that we will sell their grain, and that is what we are doing. This year we have prospects of increased export sales over last year, when our share of world markets went up.
Let me talk about specific customers. China bought less grain in total last year than it bought in the previous year, but it bought approximately the same amount from Canada. This means that our percentage of their requirements went up. That is not a failure, that is a success story. It would be useful if Hon. Members used some of those facts on the record to put their remarks in a better context.
Let me indicate what happened with exports. At the end of August and the beginning of September in Vancouver, this country hosted a food exhibition for the first time. It was called Food Pacific 86. Its purpose was to bring all the countries in the Pacific region together at an international exposition of food products to let the world know what we had to offer. It was an absolutely resounding success. We give a lot of credit to the British Columbia Government for initiating this exposition and a lot of credit to many people in the federal Government who worked very hard. Eighty-one countries, provinces and various forms of Governments were represented. There were over 800 exhibitors, and some 25,000 buyers attended in four days. Does that sound like a Government and country that is not concerned or doing anything about agricultural exports? Perhaps we can do more, but the Opposition does no service to anyone, above all the farmers who we are here to represent, when it suggests that we have been doing nothing.
I do not wish to prolong the debate, I simply want to put some facts on the record in order to balance the debate. We talk a lot about the U.S. Farm Bill. There is no doubt that we believe it causes problems, but I think the major problem is still with the European Community. No matter how one looks at it, they have increased their production in percentage terms more than anyone else. They have done this through continual
Canagrex
subsidies, not only with respect to grain and oil seeds but with almost every agricultural product, including dairy products, pork, beef, wine, grain and sugar-beets.
I know it is fashionable for the Opposition to be antiAmerican, but if they want to be honest and consistent they must talk about the Europeans in context with the Americans. They should not continue to blame the United States. They should give credit to the Americans when they deserve it. While we may have disagreements with the Americans, they have offered to put their U.S. Farm Bill on the table if the Europeans will agree to do the same. We have yet to see such an offer come from the European Community. If the Europeans were willing to discuss the problem as openly as the Americans, we could make some progress.
We have expressed our doubts to the Americans that the U.S. Farm Bill is working. We told them that they will not get markets simply on the basis of price alone. This has been borne out by the BICEP Program since it was introduced in May, 1985. I can send Hon. Members opposite copies of speeches I have made in the United States in which I have pointed this out to them directly. However, I believe that the main culprit is still the Europeans. The average increase in wheat production by the Europeans since 1968-69 has been almost 20 per cent. They started with a larger base than Canada. The average increase in the United States is 13.3 per cent. This points out again that the major problem in cereal production world-wide is the European Community. Canada comes third with a 3.5 per cent increase since 1968-69, and Australia and Argentina increases are smaller than Canada's.
When we have a debate like this and talk about the very serious problems which face a very productive sector of our economy, I would very much like to have some balance. I think if we could have that balance we might get some useful suggestions from the opposition. We, as a Government, have shown a willingness to sit down and work with people and listen to ideas. If members of the Opposition have some useful ideas we would be more than happy to listen to them. I would like to suggest that if all the Opposition is going to do is take a one-sided, narrow, partisan and political approach, it will not be helpful to any of us, especially the farmers we represent.

I think this is an excellent opportunity now, Madam Speaker, to hear what the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board has to say. Of course, this Bill deals with practically all farm commodities besides those commodities handled by the Canadian Wheat Board, so the Minister was slightly off topic. But this is such a sterling opportunity to make some comments about the subject that I would not want to miss doing so.
The Minister talks about the great things he has done. He certainly did something last spring when he announced the initial price for wheat, which was $130 per tonne. That is the lowest wheat price since the 1930s in real dollars. He sort of skipped over that and told us about the wonderful meetings he

October 21, 1986
Canagrex
held and about the meetings he tried to hold around the world. But he did not mention the grinding reality of wheat prices, the lowest since the 1930s. The response of the Government to that reality has been negligible, if not non-existent.
The Minister said he wanted some useful suggestions. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and I met with the presidents of the Prairie Wheat Pool in Regina in mid-May. We recommended that there be a deficiency payment. Every other farm organization I know of has also recommended a deficiency payment. We received a glancing kind of commitment from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), mostly aimed at assisting the Premier of Saskatchewan, in the Address and Reply to the Speech from the Throne, but we still do not have any specific commitment as to whether we are going to get a deficiency payment, some kind of aid program or some kind of guaranteed program, or whatever. We made that suggestion some five months ago. Every prairie premier and every farm organization has been suggesting it since then. But five months down the pipe we still have no specifics as to whether there will be a deficiency payment, whether there is going to be some loan guarantee or, indeed, anything is going to be provided in spite of the lowest grain prices in 50 years in real dollar terms.

Madam Speaker, I have just a few comments. The Minister said in his address to us today that we have criticized his Government unfairly, and perhaps upon occasion we are rather severe at criticizing the Government. However, I think it deserves a fair level of criticism because, of course, it gave itself the mandate it did; it made the 338 Tory promises which you and I, Madam Speaker, have had to listen to. Those promises are on PC logo letterhead and those promises are what I want to bring to the attention of the Minister today.
Perhaps to expect a Government to live up to its commitment is something that is beyond reality. However, that is not for us in opposition to decide. This is something the Government has created for itself and I think it owes it to Canadians to issue some kind of revised list of promises, telling Canadians that it has now decided that 229 of the 338 promises never should have been made and it apologizes for making them to start with. But as long as that list holds, it is our job to hold this Government accountable for what it said it would do, for what it is doing and for what it is not doing.
The Minister said to us today that the Government had done some things well and, in particular, in the year 1985 it had increased commodity sales. I pointed out to him, and 1 am sorry I interrupted him to do so that it was before the U.S. Farm Bill, but he said it was after. I would like the Minister to be a little more precise on that answer. If the U.S. Farm Bill was passed on December 23, 1985, and the Minister said those sales were for 1985 after the U.S. Farm Bill, were those sales between December 24 and December 31, because there were only seven days left in the year at the time the U.S. President signed his Bill into law?

Madam Speaker, I can certainly respond to that. The Hon. Member should know that the BISEP program, which is still the export enhancement arm of the U.S. Farm Bill, was introduced in June of 1985. That is over a year ago. This is October of 1986. The crop year that we base statistics on for our wheat exports starts on August 1, 1985, some two months after the BISEP program was introduced. So the crop year to which I was referring runs from August 1, 1985, to July 31, 1986, for which time-the full-time-the BISEP program was in effect. It was in effect two months prior to the beginning of the crop year for which I quoted the Hon. Members statistics. If the Hon. Member wants to do his homework, and be a little less willing to jump to conclusions which assume the worst, he would know that Canada has increased its exports of wheat in spite of some very massive amounts of money the U.S. Government has been spending to try to increase its market. We have been successful. No one has said prices are good. There is no room for joy as far as prices are concerned; we know that. We are attempting to address that on the international scene with discussions, with GATT, and so on. We have been successful in selling, which is entirely different from what happened in the early 1970s when the previous Government walked out on Canadian farmers. It told them not to grow. It introduced the LIFT program which hurt our exports and our reputation as a reliable supplier. We have no intention of seeing that happen this time around because we are going to do our very best to sell the grain Canadian farmers produce.
I should also say that when we talk about grain, it is genuinely a Canadian problem. Ontario is the third largest producer of grain in this country, following Saskatchewan and Alberta, and then my home Province of Manitoba. So it is a national issue and we are addressing it as such.

Mr. Speaker, I thought the Minister might respond and make it clear whether there was going to be a deficiency payment for Canadian grain producers, exactly how much it will be and when it will be announced. The Saskatchewan election is over. The vagueness has been played out. It seems to me it is now up to the Government to announce clearly just what the deficiency payment will be, whether it will be cash, on what basis it will be paid, whether it will be on an acreage basis or delivery basis. I think it would be really helpful if the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board, since he is here and is asking for suggestions and ideas, could make that clear. He has talked about how there was no incentive in the early 1970s. I ask him now, where is the great incentive for grain producers in Canada today when grain prices are the lowest they have been since the 1930s? Grain is now being sold at $130 per tonne and today, on October 21, there are still no quotas for even one bushel of grain in most rural delivery points.

Madam Speaker, with respect to the last comment of the Hon. Member, he should know that there is no
October 21, 1986

question that quotas are slow in coming this year, for a couple of reasons. First, there were several quotas announced at the beginning of last week. Last Friday there were general quotas of approximately three bushels for the whole Wheat Board area. So there are some quotas.
Second, the Hon. Member should also know that there are some very good grain movements planned for between now and freeze-up in the St. Lawrence going east, and there are some heavy sales commitments that the Canadian Wheat Board and others have going out to the West Coast. So we look for some pretty substantial movement of grain between now and Christmas, which is certainly good news.
I would like to make it clear that there are quotas, admittedly longer in coming than any of us would have liked, but there are certainly quotas in place now.
With regard to the deficiency payment, I do not know what else 1 can say in this regard. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has talked about $1 billion. We have said that it will be additional money for agriculture and that no existing program will be cut. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has said it is not a loan guarantee.
In my view, there was no confusion in the minds of the Saskatchewan farmers who went to the polls yesterday and voted. Everyone understands that this Government has made a firm commitment and intends on following through with it in as fair and as equitable a fashion as we possibly can, and as quickly as we possibly can.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Next time when the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) wants a reply, perhaps he could make his question or comment a little shorter. This time I let the Minister reply, but we are about one minute over time. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet).

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make my contribution to the debate on Bill C-2, an Act to dissolve Canagrex, and a piece of legislation which I personally find very regrettable.
We are often asked what the fundamental difference is between the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party. I think this is an excellent opportunity to demonstrate clearly the difference between the two major political parties. The Liberal Party has always taken the position that it is important to have Crown corporations in order to help our economy develop in certain areas where the private sector either does not have the will or the means or simply does not have an opportunity to be active. Consequently, Crown corporations are supposed to play a supplemental role in supporting the Canadian economy, acting as a complement to the private sector. It is clear that the Conservative Government has an entirely different philosophy. It is against Crown corporations. What it wants, and I cannot blame it for doing so, since during the last election campaign, the Conservatives clearly said they wanted
Canagrex
to sell and dismantle a number of Crown corporations and let the private sector take over. However, I think this Bill is a mistake. I agree it is in line with the commitment made by the Conservatives to dismantle a Crown corporation. However, the question we must ask today is: Is the Government right to follow up that commitment?
We have just heard the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board make an excellent speech, explaining the work of the Board whose role is to sell Canadian wheat, mostly produced by farmers in western Canada, on foreign markets.
When the previous Liberal Government decided to create Canagrex, farmers in Eastern Canada, especially in my own province, the Province of Quebec, were very much in favour of this plan, because the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec was telling us at the time: Why do we have a Crown corporation that promotes the concerns of Western producers and sells western wheat throughout the world, while we have no corporation to market farm products from Quebec or the Maritimes or to bring the products of UPA members to international markets?
Canagrex was established by the former Liberal administration in a climate of open opposition. When the then Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, introduced the Bill the Conservative Party opposite government benches did indeed raise very strong objections. As you may recall, companies like Canada Packers with offices practically in every country around the world-not necessarily to sell Canadian products, but rather to promote their own interests-were adamant in their opposition to the creation of a corporation like Canagrex which in certain cases might step on the international scene and operate in a way which a company such as Canada Packers would not necessarily appreciate.
Still the majority of Members of Parliament endorsed the creation of this Crown corporation because they knew that many small farmers throughout Canada would at long last have an agency like Canagrex to defend their interests, and market and sell their products for them in foreign countries. As a matter of fact, a farmer from the riding of Rimouski, Montmagny or Drummond simply cannot go and sell his own products abroad, but another one from Weyburn, Moose Jaw or Manitoba can indeed expect an agency like the Canadian Wheat Board to sell his wheat overseas.
Why should an eastern Canada producer not be able to rely on a national agency or a Crown corporation to sell his products on foreign markets?
Obviously I am disappointed that the Conservative Members should be seeking to put the axe to this agency set up by the previous administration and losing all interest in providing fair service to all farmers anywhere in Canada through a Crown corporation whose mandate is unmistakable.
I can only conclude that Canagrex was never given a real chance to become operative: The moment this Government

October 21, 1986
Canagrex
took office it did everything possible to get rid of the corporation, and this Bill is the best evidence of that.
The Government of Canada is not alone in trying to sell products abroad. I have only to quote what Minister Whelan said when Canagrex was established to remind the House that nearly every country has agencies or programs to assist farmers.
It is therefore regrettable that the Conservative Government would want to remove this tool from Canadian agricultural producers, especially the members of the Union des produc-teurs agricoles, who were relying on the assistance of Canagrex.
If I may quote what Minister Whelan said at the time:
The United States of America, with more than $36 billion in agricultural and food exports in 1979, has a number of tools, such as its Foreign Agriculture Service, the Co-operative Program, and the Commodity Credit Corporation-
Those are there to help the American farmer. It goes on:
You can see the other programs that other countries have by their different names.
France, for instance, has SOPEXA, Denmark, the Agriculture Marketing Board-Germany has the CM A; Britain, the British Overseas Trade Board; Australia, the Export Development Council Commodity Board; Israel, Agrexco; Mexico, Conasupo.

Naturally, all these Government agencies play a role to help farmers in their own countries. The previous Liberal Government believed that a national agency such as Canagrex could play a vital role in helping Canadian farm producers, to complement the role already played by certain private organizations. I find it regrettable that the Conservative Government now wants to rely only on private initiative to sell our farm products abroad, except for Canadian wheat.
I therefore close by asking this question: If it is now, has been in the past and will continue to be in the future a good thing to sell Canadian wheat abroad, why would a similar agency not be just as useful in selling other products, such as beef, poultry, fruits, and vegetables in other countries in the best interests of Canadian farmers?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway).

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. He will know that he is the sixth Member of his Party to speak on this particular piece of legislation. He and all of the other Members of his Party who spoke prior to him made quite clear the position of the Liberal Party with respect to this Bill. There is another piece of legislation designed to assist farmers, which is the next matter on the Order Paper for this morning and that, of course, is Bill C-12,
an Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to put more money into the hands of agriculture.
I know the Hon. Member represents an urban riding, as I do. In fact, the Hon. Member at one time was the Minister of Urban Affairs. I am sure he really does have the best interests of Canadian farmers at heart. I wonder if he would urge his colleagues to not put up any further speakers to filibuster this Bill but to get on with its quick passage so that we can deal with the next Bill to put money into the hands of Canadian farmers. I know the Hon. Member wants to do that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know the Hon. Member to be reasonable, and a gentleman. I do not think he should be imputing motives or blaming us for filibustering the Bill. We are discussing an important Bill.
We did not impute motives to Conservative Members when we spent two days discussing Bill C-ll last week. We did not mind the Conservative Party putting up everyone it could find to have Throne Speech debates put on the record. We did not say that Conservative Members were filibustering Bill C-ll. I cannot believe that the Hon. Member was serious when he said that we are filibustering the Canagrex Bill.

Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) well knows, the rules of the House provide for a certain set time to debate the Speech from the Throne. Irrespective of whether the Government wants to proceed with legislation quickly or slowly, there is no way it can do so given the requirements of the Standing Orders of the House with respect to the debate on the Speech from the Throne. Of course, that does not apply to this Bill. That is why I am sure the Hon. Member would agree that his Party should get on with the next piece of legislation rather than filibuster this one.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Hon. Members have a right to debate this Bill. I think the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) knows that very well. It was not a point of order on his part.

Madam Speaker, I would like to reply to the Hon. Member who seems to find it surprising that six Liberal Members would take part in the debate on Bill C-2. Naturally, the Liberal Party, which created Canagrex under the previous administration is very sad to see it disappear, and I do not think that anyone in this House will blame us for expressing our disagreement, for reminding the Government of the reasons why this Crown Corporation was created, and, most important, for saying why we think that the Government should not go forward with this Bill. There is a saying that if you repeat something often enough, something might come of it. It seems obvious to me that on this matter government Members have their ears plugged, which means we have to repeat over and over again, and go on repeating if we are to get some sense into them, if we are to get them to make better decisions for Canadians.

October 21, 1986

So it is clear to me, Madam Speaker, that the Hon. Member is not aware how seriously involved 1 was with farm groups in the Province of Quebec. For 15 years 1 have been meeting periodically with representatives of the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, and Madam Speaker would know full well that I often travelled to her constituency, because the Saint-Hyacinthe area has one of the major and more progressive farm producers' associations and our Government in the past has always been very sensitive to the recommendations and suggestions from the Union des producteurs agricoles, and in co-operation with them we have implemented things that were very important in the Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot area, to the benefit of farm producers.
1 know that this debate is of great concern in many ways to thousands of farm producers, small farmers who hoped that a large corporation such as Canagrex could provide easier access to markets and, above all, since market forces would have it that if you are a corporation such as Canada Packers dealing with a small beef producer and you are probably the only domestic buyer, that farmer is at a tremendous disadvantage to sell his product. Which means in the final analysis that the seller has to accept the buyer's price. On the other hand, with a corporation like Canagrex that could have acted as a globetrotting agent or salesman for a multitude of small producers, it could have been a seller's price, rather than a buyer's, as it is often the case with a large multinational corporation, whose concern is far more for profits than for the survival of the Quebec farmer and farming industry.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions, comments? Debate.
I now recognize the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).

Madam Speaker, as a few of my colleagues who have not yet risen in your presence, I would first like to congratulate you on your appointment to the Chair and offer our support in your difficult task, because working in the Chair is truly demanding. Having gone through two decades of Speakers, I can say, Madam Speaker, that you have the potential for being one of the best. Congratulations!
If the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) is right about the numbers, and he always is, I am the eighth Liberal to speak today on this debate on the dissolution of Canagrex. It is a very bad decision by the Government. As the Hon. Member knows, if eight of us are rising, that is certainly not enough to keep this important Crown corporation alive. The Conservative Government will have its way. The company will be dissolved. But, the Hon. Member should not begrudge us the opportunity, which is limited by our small numbers, to put on the record the great hopes that we and a very large constituency of Canadians, particularly in the agricultural sector, had for this corporation.
I do not want to belabour arguments, lists, and so on, that other Hon. Members have put forward. I hope the Hon.
Canagrex
Member for York East was here when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) read the large number of agricultural sector organizations that were in favour of Canagrex and felt that Canagrex could play a part in taking the products of Canada's agricultural sector to world markets. It was a very long list, including bee keepers, grain dealers, all types of livestock dealers. I had not heard that list before. 1 was impressed to hear that support for the Bill when it was brought forward by our former colleague, Eugene Whelan, when he was Minister of Agriculture, and that so many voices from the agricultural community were asking for exactly this type of a selling agent for their goods.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) are here. The experience of the Canadian Wheat Board ought to have demonstrated to the Conservatives that an agency like this can do the job. If the Government wanted to be consistent, it would be wanting to abolish the Wheat Board. The Government knows that an attempt to abolish the Wheat Board would meet resistance. If only it had the foresight to see that the potential of Canagrex is larger than the potential of the Canadian Wheat Board, it would support it. It is not their style to try and look ahead. The style of the Conservatives is to cut, cut, cut Government out of an ideology. This is not something that costs a great deal of money, but it is something that has a lot of potential. Yet, they want to cut it because of ideology. They will be going to the people in the next election with a list. There is a constituency out there that wants to see Government savaged, wants to see as much reduction as possible. Anything that the Government can discard, any responsibility that can be taken away from it, is to the good. We are dealing with a fringe of public opinion that feels that the less Government there is the better. Sometimes there is too much Government, but sometimes there is too little. In this area of world marketing of agricultural products I do not think there is enough. I think Canagrex is needed. It had the support, it had a role, and it was off to a good start. Good people were recruited to make it work. The Government wanted to add one more to the list in its ideological commitment of so-called achievements of demolition and destruction of vital organs that serve the Canadian people. Canagrex was so young it could be destroyed with less damage than the destruction of some other agencies that maybe are not doing such an important job, or maybe do not have the kind of potential that Canagrex had. The Government considered it an easy kill in the list of Crown corporations. The Liberals cannot let that pass. We came to the decision to establish Canagrex after a lot of thought and consultation.
I would like to remind the House what Canagrex was doing. It was to provide market identification and intelligence; to offer promotion and information services; to provide loans and guarantees; to enter into joint ventures with private companies, marketing boards and co-operatives; to act as an agent of the Crown in negotiating state-to-state contracts.

October 21, 1986
If I can stop in this long list of functions that was to be performed by Canagrex on that role of acting in the negotiation of state-to-state contracts, you will see the kind of function that this corporation of the Crown would have provided that cannot be provided by Canada Packers, Burns Brothers, or all of the different heavy hitters in agriculture. If those companies had seen the Government decision to estabish Canagrex in the proper terms, they could have been part of the promotion of Canagrex, and made money on it at the same time as farmers were benefiting from finding larger markets for their products.
Another important function of Canagrex was to provide grants and contributions to help accelerate product development, promotion, or the provision of needed infrastructure. A Crown corporation has a much longer horizon than a private company. It does not try to maximize profits in the short term, or consider itself responsible for the assets of which it holds the title. A Crown corporation takes a larger view of its responsibility in the economy and to the Canadian people. I remember when they were talking about cutting off-sorry, has my time expired?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have the honour to lay upon the Table the report of the Auditor General of Canada to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1986. I remind Hon. Members that, under Standing Order 96(3)(f), this report is deemed to have been permanently referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, in a statement under Standing Order 21, on the budget of Environment Canada, I inadvertently neglected to deduct the budget of the Canadian Forestry Service transferred to Agriculture Canada in 1985. To take this transfer into account, the 1984 budget of Environment Canada should read $741 million, not $886 million. This year's Environment Canada's budget shows $745 million, $3.6 million more than the 1984 budget.
To avoid the erosion caused by inflation at 4.2 per cent per year, in 1985 there should have been an increase of $31 million in Environment Canada's budget amounting to $772 million, and again in 1986 an increase of $32 million amounting to $805 million. At a time when Canadians are asking the Government to play a stronger role in the environment, there is a slippage of $59.9 million over the past two years in Environment Canada's purchasing power, without counting budget cuts.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA PORTS DISPUTE OVER HANDLING OF CONTAINER CARGO
BRITISH COLUMBIA PORTS DISPUTE OVER HANDLING OF CONTAINER CARGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would remind Members of this House that the time clock is ticking for a negotiated settlement in the ports of British Columbia, particularly with regard to the container clause. When the clause was negotiated in 1970 it was expected that it would maximize work opportunities for longshoremen, but to some extent it has had the opposite effect. In 1980 containers bound for Canada via Seattle/Tacoma amounted to 30,000 units, and via Vancouver 55,313 units. By 1984 these figures were 79,600 units via Seattle/Tacoma, and for Vancouver 66,300 units, an increase of 165 per cent and 19.9 per cent respectively.
In the report of the Conciliation Commissioner, Donald Larson points out that were it not for the container clause a large number of the containers shipped through Seattle/Tacoma and then trans-shipped by truck to Vancouver would be shipped through the Port of Vancouver. He recommends the removal of article 26:05, the container clause, and suggests a guaranteed number of hours to cover this clause.
I urge both parties in their meetings to use the report's recommendations as the basis for settlement.
October 21, 1986

Mr. Speaker, soon it will be six months since the report of the subcommittee on CN pensions reported back to the House through the transport committee. The ball has been in the Government's court with respect to this issue now for almost half a year.
I want to take this opportunity to call on the Government to indicate to the House and to the many tens of thousands of CN pensioners just what it intends to do about this particular issue. It is an issue that has been long studied by the House. Great expectations were raised by the striking of the subcommittee. I know that not all pensioners were happy with every jot and tittle of the report. Nevertheless, it remains the case that a great many things were recommended by that subcommittee which, if implemented by the Government, would be to the great benefit of pensioners and people in active service at the CNR.
1 call on the Government to act with respect to this issue that has been before the House for so long, and to indicate to pensioners and to railway workers just what the Tories intend to do about something that they very often said when in opposition they would do something about.

subtopic: FINANCIAL NEEDS OF ELDERLY SINGLE WOMEN
FINANCIAL NEEDS OF ELDERLY SINGLE WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government had made real progress toward the goal of ensuring that all Canadians enjoy a secure retirement. Pension plans are now more portable and we have made it easier for individuals to save for retirement through RRSPs. More than
50,000	older people, mostly women, have a higher income today because we made the spouse's allowance available to all financially needy widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. Another 35,000 Canadians, again mostly women, have recovered the Canada Pension Plan survivor benefits they initially lost when they remarried.
The system is substantially better than it was but there is still room for improvement, particularly in the case of divorced or never married women who are therefore not eligible to receive the spouse's allowance. We must recognize the contribution which women make as individuals and provide a decent standard of living for all women regardless of their marital status. While their circumstances may be different from those of widows and widowers, the financial needs of older women who are divorced or who have never married are just as real.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-WITHDRAWAL BY GENERAL MOTORS CORPORATION
SOUTH AFRICA-WITHDRAWAL BY GENERAL MOTORS CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to take note of the decision by General Motors to pull out of South Africa. GM, the largest U.S. operation in South Africa, took its decision essentially for three reasons: first, a disappointment with the pace of dismantling apartheid; secondly, the recent imposition of stricter U.S. trade sanctions against South Africa; thirdly, the adverse effect on domestic sales resulting from GM's presence in South Africa. It is also worth noting that this is a company from which originated the Sullivan principles dealing with codes of conduct.
The American people are to be congratulated for having mobilized an effective campaign against apartheid which, two weeks ago, forced the hand of a President and now that of the largest corporation in the world. There is a message in this for Canadians opposed to apartheid. When people join together to act according to their convictions, even the mighty will fall into line with what is right. The corporations of Canada should take note, as should the Government of Canada which should not weaken in its resolve to provide leadership in the struggle against apartheid.

Mr. Speaker, the recently published Federal Government Reporting Study done jointly by the office of the Auditor General of Canada and the United States General Accounting office is a most useful document. The Public Sector Accounting and Auditing Committee of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants has, as have many parliamentarians, been advocating more useful, understandable, reliable and relevant financial reporting. The study, if implemented, will take us a long way toward these goals. In particular, the illustrative annual financial report of the Government of Canada, with its three consolidated statements of operations, financial requirements, and financial position, provides information in a useful, broad, and complete way. It is to be hoped that this new reporting format might be used on a continuing basis for part of the Public Accounts of Canada.

NON-PAYMENT OF INCOME TAX BY CREDIT FONCIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to announce today the seventh winner of our great untaxed corporation award. Today's award goes to Credit Foncier. That company has been granted by successive Liberal and Conservative Governments, through tax concessions, the right to claim tax credits in 1979 and 1982 on millions of dollars of profits. In 1980, 1981, 1983 and 1984, when it did pay current corporation taxes, the tax rate was so low it was almost nonexistent, only an average of 1.5 per cent.
Had the tax system been fair and had Credit Foncier been required to pay a tax rate of even 25 per cent on its more than $43 million in profits since 1979, taxpaying Canadians would have paid $10.3 million less in taxes because of this one company alone. We hope this reminder to the Government will result in an immediate, real, comprehensive tax reform.

speechtext:

that Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is no secret that we face some very difficult times in the grain and oilseeds business, not only around the world, but especially in Canada. This Government has been attempting to respond to that situation in several ways.
We face some serious problems largely because of the subsidies offered by the European Economic Community, and the U.S. Farm Bill that has resulted in literally a trade war that has driven down the prices worldwide, and as a result has driven down the prices to our producers. This problem has been coming for some time. The only long-term solution to this problem is to have it addressed and looked at internationally. What the countries in the European Economic Community do within their own borders is entirely their own affair. However, when they are able to increase their production dramatically through subsidies, and on that basis become very competitive with us for some of the international markets that Canada has traditionally been able to supply, we have legitimate reason to make observations and to complain about that situation. That is precisely what has been happening.
Our farmers are very efficient. We have a good climate and soil and in many respects we enjoy significant competitive advantage, or comparative advantage, in economic terms. That allows us to produce a very high quality product that is in demand around the world. What is increasingly difficult for our farmers is to be able to compete with the treasuries of the European Economic Community and the United States.
I would like to give you a couple of examples as to why that is difficult. First of all, looking at the average income dollar that a Canadian farmer has, about 50 cents out of every dollar come from exports. Using these same criteria in the United States, about 25 cents of every income dollar that a farmer has come from exports. On that basis, exports are very important to the Canadian farmer. Looking at some of the specific commodities, grain and wheat, in Canada we export roughly
October 21, 1986

80 per cent of all the wheat that we grow. About 10 per cent is used in domestic consumption in bread, cookies and pastry. The remaining 10 per cent is used for seed, industrial use, feed, and those purposes. In the European Economic Community, the figure is almost exactly reversed. The European farmer is only reliant on exports for 20 per cent of his production. In other words, 80 per cent of the European farmer's production of wheat is consumed within the European Economic Community. On that basis, as far as wheat is concerned, in comparison to the European Economic Community, Canada is very dependent on exports.
Some of the subsidies that the Europeans currently have available to them are very large. In the southern Prairies we produce Durum wheat, which is second in quality to none in the world. It is as good as any. It is very high quality grain. Our farmers this year are receiving $130 per metric tonne as an initial payment. The European farmers are receiving $450 per metric tonne. On that basis, it then becomes very difficult for the Canadian farmer to deal with that. It is not because we are inefficient; it is because we have a smaller population on which to rely for a domestic market. Therefore, we are much more reliant on exports. That is why this Government has taken the lead in addressing some of these problems at the international level.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) visited Japan for the Tokyo Summit in May, he raised agricultural trade and subsidies as Canada's agenda item. That is the first time that had ever happened. A month later I had the opportunity to host the four other major wheat exporting countries. This was the first time ever that such a meeting had been held in Canada. It was held at Whistler, in British Columbia. The five major wheat exporting countries meet regularly to discuss problems at the bureaucratic level, but this was the first time such a meeting had been held at the political level. In August, Canada also participated in an international meeting at Cairns, Australia, prior to the agenda setting GATT at Uruguay, in which Canada played a major role. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) gave the lead-off speech and set the tone for the meeting. The result was that agriculture was included on the GATT agenda for the first time in the seven meetings that had been held. We are making some progress there. Unfortunately, that progress is slow and it will take time. In the meantime, our farmers need to have some support.
We have supported our farmers in many respects. We removed the tax on farm fuel. We froze freight rates this year. The grain commission froze the maximum tariffs under which the grain companies operate. We amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act to provide assistance at a more opportune time during the year. If there is going to be a triggering of a pay-out under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the money is available prior to spring seeding when farmers need it the most. This amendment was put through the House in February of 1985. Many initiatives have been taken on the agricultural
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
side in terms of supporting our producers, and especially our grain producers.
One of the other things that we are doing is to support the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board, plus private institutions that market our grain and oil seeds. The record shows that over the past crop year, Canada increased its sales over the previous crop year. In 1985-86 we exported over 2 million tonnes more than we did in the previous crop year. At the end of the crop year, which is on July 31, our farmers went into the new crop year with the lowest on-farm carry-over ever. That is a result of sales.
Canada now has long-term sales agreements that total more tonnes than any other wheat exporting country. We have a long-term grain sales with Egypt which runs for five years. That was signed in the spring of 1985. We concluded a three-year term with Brazil. Last month we renewed a major longterm sales agreement with the Soviet Union. That is certainly good news for Canadian farmers in these very difficult times. Again, just to emphasize, price is still a major problem and there is not a lot of room for optimism. On the volume side we did very well last year. We increased our share of world wheat markets. With the sales program that is in place for this crop year, if it holds up for the rest of the crop year, we have the potential to increase our grain sales this year and our percentage of world grain markets.
I have here a clipping from The Ottawa Citizen of October 3 that talks about the Soviet grain deal. It shows a picture of the Prime Minister and the Soviet Foreign Minister. The caption reads "U.S.S.R. Signs Five Year Grain Deal". Seeing a Prime Minister of Canada in a newspaper in conjunction with a longterm grain sales agreement is something I find refreshing after what we had from previous Governments, their attitudes about grain and how they approached the problem. This is an encouraging sign. To see the Prime Minister's picture in the paper seems entirely natural and appropriate based on the record of our Government in dealing with agricultural problems.
This brings me to the Bill at hand. It is a Bill to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. It is a Bill that was first introduced and passed by the Progressive Conservative Government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker in 1957. I see the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), a distinguished Member of this House and a distinguished former Minister of Agriculture here in the House. He is the one who was responsible for starting the wheat sales with the People's Republic of China. He has made a great contribution not only to this House but to Canadian agriculture in general. He informs me that the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act was one of the first pieces of legislation to be introduced by the Diefenbaker Government in 1957. It has served farmers very well and it is being used more and more.

October 21, 1986
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
We are introducing today some amendments to this Act to make it more responsive to farmer's needs to help them deal with their cash flow situation. Let me explain what this Bill does. When farmers harvest grain, it takes considerable time to market it. Depending on weather, harvest season lasts a month in the Wheat Board area. Farmers will harvest all their grain in a month and the grain will then be sold throughout the remainder of the year. The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act provides a cash advance for grain which the farmers have already harvested and have in store against the day when they can sell it. It is a way for farmers to realize cash once they have harvested their grain before having the opportunity to sell it. The Government provides the cash advances interest-free. The interest charges are picked up and the Canadian Wheat Board administers the Act.
What we are doing today in giving this Bill second reading is streamlining it. Upon review of the Act the Government found that changes in the administration of this legislation should be made, changes that would make the program more timely and more responsive to the needs of those who are using the Bill. I will list what the proposed amendments will do, Madam Speaker.
One of the amendments will make the Act fairer in the sense that presently producers are able to acquire cash advances based on a quota factor or on the number of acres they farm. There is no consideration for how productive is each acre that that farmer farms relative to other farmers. We are introducing an amendment to allow the cash advance to be calculated on the amount of grain a farmer has in store as opposed to the number of quota acres that he has. That will assist many producers in being able to make better use of the cash advance in the sense that the farmer will be able to get a larger cash advance if he has the productivity to back it up.
We are also proposing to amend the Act in this Bill to allow producers who have been in a default position to have their interest rates adjusted on a regular basis. There are producers who have had problems repaying loans. The default ratio though has been minimal. When you are dealing with literally tens and hundreds of thousands of producers, roughly 140,000 permit books in the Wheat Board area, you can understand that producers have problems, Mr. Speaker. There are producers who have been in default, for four or five years. Once they are in default the interest rate is set at the level of interest at that time. People who have been in default for four or five years when interest rates were 15 per cent and 16 per cent are still paying interest rates on their defaulted loan at those levels. We are proposing to amend the interest rates charged on defaulted and prepaid loans to reflect the interest rates in effect at the present time.
One of the amendments is to make it easier for farmers who are tenants to obtain a loan. Now you require the landlord's signature as well as the tenant's signature. Sometimes that takes a period of days, weeks or months and it delays the time at which a farmer can obtain a cash advance. We propose to
simplify that. Farmer tenants will now be able to sign affidavits to the effect that they have clear title to the grain grown on another's land. It will simplify things substantially and make it easier for producers to get cash advances.
Several regulations of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act must be amended each year even though these amendments are routinely and largely administrative in nature. This process takes time and in many cases too much time. We propose to remove these administrative hold-ups so that needless red tape does not come between the farmer and the advance payment.
The Canadian Wheat Board will be responsible for final approval of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act application form which changes little from year to year. Presently we have to go through an Order in Council every year to approve a form which does not vary very much from-year to year. We are going to simplify that.
We are also going to simplify the emergency provisions under the Act whereby cash advances are made available for unthrashed grain after November 15 if there is a significant amount of grain that has not been harvested. Producers can obtain a cash advance against grain that is unharvested and still in the field. Producers are also eligible for cash advances to assist in drying costs. We want to improve the administration so that those things can be done without an Order in Council and so make the whole thing easier.
We are also introducing an amendment that will give producers equitable access to cash advances right across the country.
Another amendment that I think will be welcomed by producers is that as the Canadian Wheat Board administers the Act it will have greater latitude in dealing with producers who have defaulted but who can show that extraordinary circumstances prevented them from being able to deliver against their cash advances. You run into situations in the spring with a road or a bridge that is out, situations such as that. Presently the Act does not allow for any leniency or any interpretation in that respect. We are amending the Act to give the Canadian Wheat Board, the administrators, some latitude in dealing with extraordinary circumstances. I think that will be a very useful and welcome change as far as producers who use the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act are concerned. This would have been useful had we been able to have it in effect at the beginning of the crop year which started on August 1, Madam Speaker.
I hope the Opposition will look at this legislation very favourably and give it reasonably quick passage. There are a couple of provisions which, if we can pass this Bill without a lot of delay, can actually be of some use to producers this year. Most of the amendments will have to wait until next year before they will have full effect, but some amendments, if we can have reasonably quick passage of the Bill, will be of use to producers this year.

These amendments are being made by the Government to try to be as responsive as we possibly can to grain and oilseed producers in this very difficult time. With that, Madam Speaker, I want to conclude and thank Hon. Members in the House for their kind attention.

Madam Speaker, 1 have a few comments with regard to Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. Many of the amendments are technical and will be of great value to the agriculture producers in the west. Clearly the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has suggested we have quick passage. As I think back to all the legislation which the Minister and the Government have brought in during the last two years, 1 see that the problem has never been to get quick passage, the problem has been to get legislation into the House.
I think back to the months and months and years when the Conservative Party fought the former Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, on every little amendment that he brought in to any Bill whether Canagrex or something else. Canagrex I think was in the works for some two years. That entity would have had an opportunity to get fully functional and prove itself, but the Conservative Party was bound and bent to ensure that any legislation which the former Minister brought in would be denied passage no matter how valuable it was to the agricultural community. Certainly every Bill the Government brought in has been passed in either one or two sittings of the House, even something as complicated and detailed as the legislation dealing with Farm Debt Review Boards. That should have been brought in a year ago, as the Minister promised in July of 1985. There should have been detailed discussions for several weeks, but it was belatedly brought in in about the third week of June. We passed it in two sittings of the House. Clearly the Opposition has co-operated in passing every piece of farm legislation brought before the House, whether it be the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. The Minister does not have to ask for quick passage of his legislation because he knows that every piece of legislation he has brought before the House has been passed expeditiously.
It seems to me that although many of the provisions in this legislation before the House today are of a technical nature, they will be very valuable. Farmers with very productive soil and who produce large volumes of wheat or barley on small acreages will now be able to get a cash advance based on the amount of grain they have in storage rather than on an acreage-based formula. The idea of a floating interest rate on cash advances which bear interest is a good idea. I am amazed that the Minister waited for two years to bring in that kind of provision because it is clearly a severe hardship for farmers to be paying 14 per cent or 15 per cent, which is what interest rates were in 1982 and 1983, and they are still paying them
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
today. One of the election promises made by the Government was to provide adequate funding for current day interest rates.
1 am also glad to see the amendment relating to cash advances being made available to people who lease or rent farms. It seems to me that the swearing of an affidavit by the producers concerned is adequate protection for the Government.
Then we have the emergency provisions. The Minister raised this with me last spring. He wanted to have simply an order by the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board in order to allow cash advances. I think that is a good decision. There is a provision which says that a farmer can only receive a $30,000 cash advance based on the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Agricultural Products Marketing Act in total. I would like to hear the details when the Minister is before the committee. It seems to me that the idea of an escape clause related to farmers in distress through an emergency situation and being unable to make a delivery is a good move as well.
I must say I was very struck with the Minister's comments regarding how rapidly the Government has responded to the agricultural emergency. Although he seems to believe that most of the problem lies with the European Economic Community, clearly the bottom fell out from under the grain prices when the U.S. Farm Bill was introduced. The Americans are determined to win back their share of the international market, both from us and from the EEC. Although both trading groups are probably equally at fault for falling grain prices, clearly the impact of the U.S. Farm Bill has been most dramatic for our farmers. Some economic forecasters say that net farm income will drop by 20 per cent as a result. If that is the case, it certainly will be the most Draconian measure ever used against the Canadian farm industry by any foreign Government.
I must say that I do not share the Minister's view that the Government is moving dramatically to help farmers. It seems to me that every responsible farm group in the country has been arguing for six or eight months now that there should be some kind of deficiency payment. We will be interested to see when the Government gets around to actually announcing that payment.

On October 6 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke in the House in response to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner). He referred to the desperate situation of prairie farmers. Later that afternoon outside the House the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said that this was an aid program rather than a deficiency payment, that it might be a loan guarantee or something else. The Prime Minister was certainly doing his best to talk about something that might have been interpreted in Saskatchewan as a deficiency payment. The Minister of Agriculture was backped-dling just as fast in the other direction.
The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) tries to tell us how great it is going to be. No one wants to be pessimistic. We all want to be optimistic. However, we do not see very much action by the Government. Everyone in the grain business says that there must be some kind of assistance. Probably less than 50 per cent of the grain this year will be No. 1 or No. 2. Our farmers cannot be producing grain for $3 a bushel while their friends and neighbours across the line in Montana and North Dakota are getting $6 a bushel. The difference is essentially a deficiency payment. The Government may have a deficiency payment, but it certainly will not talk about a deficiency payment. Government Members talk about farm aid and so on.
In the Auditor General's report I see a deficiency in the Western Grain Stabilization account of $100 million. That account was built up from 1979 to 1984 to almost $1 billion. Today it has a $100 million deficit. The Auditor General is calling upon the Western Grain Stabilization fund to brief the Minister fully on the financial implications of its interpretation of the method of calculating the stabilization payments to be made under the Western Grain Stabilization Act and to obtain specific approval to use this and any other interpretation.
It may be that $500 million or $600 million will be put into the Western Grain Stabilization fund in order that the interim payment can be approved next February or March. Similar payments may be made under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. That will simply be the deficiency funding which the Prime Minister has been promising for the benefit of the Saskatchewan election. I submit it would be very greatly misleading to the House if that were proposed. We have seen the Western Grain Stabilization fund drop over $1 billion in the last couple of years. If that is what he is doing, it is out and out deception. That would not be surprising.
I was really surprised that the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board dared to mention the Prime Minister's announcement of April 30. If there was ever a smoke and mirrors, shabby piece of work by a desperate Prime Minister, it was certainly that announcement of $200 million or $300 million which he made here in Ottawa. I hope that the $1 billion of aid for western grain producers which we are now talking about is more real than the phoney announcement the Prime Minister made on April 30 before leaving on his trip to Asia with his maid and butler. That $1 million could have well been spent for western agriculture.
That announcement had three elements. First, it announced an increase in the range of the domestic price of wheat from $7 to $11. Many people thought that farmers were going to get an increase from $7 to $11 a tonne for grain sold for domestic purposes. A $4 per bushel increase would have amounted to almost $300 million a year. The press release aggregated all these figures and said that farmers will get another $300 million increase in the domestic price of wheat. That is, of course, totally phoney. It is irresponsible. It did not fool the

farmers for more than a day or so because it was quickly picked up. The Prime Minister got the headlines before he flew off on his trip to Asia, which may be good politics, but he did not fool the farmers for very long.
A recent poll showed that 70 per cent of Canadians are very concerned about the farm situation. The Prime Minister does a disservice to the rest of society, which consists of about 96 per cent of the population, because they think the farmers got $300 million through an increase in the domestic price of wheat which they did not get. The story was spun out a little bit longer. There was another announcement in July that the range was changing again. Of course, farmers never realized five cents out of it.
The second element of the Prime Minister's announcement of April 30 was that he was going to freeze the freight rates. Ele was going to show the railway companies and protect the agricultural community. It only took a couple of hours to check out that canard. We found that the Department of Transport had recalculated the volumes of grain to be shipped and there were going to be 28.5 million tonnes rather than 31 million tonnes. It was not really freezing the freight rates, but simply recalculating the volumes so that there did not have to be a freight rate increase. This is the kind of phoney announcement that is meant to suggest that the Prime Minister has done something great for agriculture. I believe the amount there was $42 million.
I hope the announcement of $1 billion in assistance will not be as phoney as the Prime Minister's announcement in April that he would remove the excise tax on farm fuels. He put on two cents a litre last September and was able to get the excise tax for the fall harvest. In Saskatchewan they called the tax imposed by the Prime Minister the harvest tax.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made that announcement on May 23, 1985, we pleaded with him to give an exemption. I asked the Minister in the House not to levy that excise tax. The Government did not want to put it on in the summer because it had so much trouble with the deindexation of the old age pension.
We pleaded with the Minister not to levy the tax because Canadian agriculture was in great difficulty, yet the Minister put on that tax just in time to pick up most of the revenues for the fall harvest. Lo and behold, in April, after everyone in western Canada had filled their fuel tanks, the Government announced it would remove that tax in May or June. He then had the audacity to announce that this would save Canadian farmers some $150 over two years. He did not say that it cost the farmers some $50 million or $60 million over the previous nine months.
If the Prime Minister really wanted to be honest with Canadians and western Canadian farmers, he would have apologized on April 30 for putting that excise tax on and then

would have removed it retroactively to September 2, 1985 when he imposed it. It is pure larceny to impose such a tax.
We are waiting with bated breath to hear whether or not the Government will provide a deficiency payment or whether it will just replenish the Western Grain Stabilization Fund which the Auditor General's Report shows has a $100 million deficit today.
We are going through an incredibly difficult time in agricultural commodities in the world right now. The Government must reduce input costs as much as possible. We probably cannot provide the kind of deficiency payments that the EEC or the United States provide to their farmers. Export sales are more important to us than they are to the EEC or the United States proportionately and the Government, regardless of its right wing, reactionary and regressive policies, has a responsibility to try to maintain the industry in a survival position during the next three years that the U.S. seems hellbent on subsidizing exports. For the Government to do less would be criminal. Hundreds of farms will be lost.
We have seen the Government dither on the question of the Farm Debt Review Board. It established a board that really has no powers except to forestall banks and credit institutions from foreclosing. Hopefully it will do some good, but the bankers got to the Minister and the Government and prevented it from providing the board with any real powers to reschedule debt.
The Minister talks about co-operation. He always has our corporation in passing good legislation. It has been four months since the legislation was passed, yet in Ontario only three members of the 10-person board have been appointed. Not one case has been heard before a debt review panel. The Government seems to move in slow motion.
However, when the banks went broke in Alberta there was immediately a back-up of $1 billion. When we talk about $1 billion for a deficiency payment for western Canada, which should be much more in order to cover the whole country, the process is dragged out for month after month. It is very similar to the commodity-based mortgage. I am sure that every Canadian who listened to the Budget Speech believed that literally thousands and thousands of farmers would receive low-interest loans at 6 per cent. In fact, $730 million was going to be provided at 6 per cent interest. However, like the Prime Minister's phoney announcement on April 30, the fine print in those commodity-based mortgages reveal that many of the farmers will not get 6 per cent interest. Even those farmers who receive 6 per cent will probably ultimately pay 2 per cent more than the current Farm Credit Corporation rate, some 12.75 per cent interest in the end. If the commodity price goes up, the interest paid is not only higher, it goes 2 per cent above the standard Farm Credit Corporation rate.
The fact that there is no new money is also disquieting. The $730 million is the same $730 million that farmers have in FCC loans now. For instance, if a farmer has a $100,000 mortgage, he is given a $100,000 mortgage here at approximately 8 per cent or 9 per cent, or 6 per cent in some cases where the equity is low enough. However, as commodity prices rise-the price of hogs has risen by 25 per cent this year-the interest rates go up dramatically. Over the course of the 10-year mortgage the farmer pays 2 per cent more than the FCC rate. The only way to get out of that mortgage is to pay out the interest right through for the full ten years at 12.75 per cent or whatever the rate is at 2 per cent above the FCC rate.
The dishonest aspect of the announcement by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board is that there is no new money. It is essentially only exchanging one FCC loan for another. If you have a 12 per cent loan with the Bank of Commerce, the Bank of Nova Scotia or the Royal Bank, tough apples, there is nothing for you. The commitment of the Government to agriculture is really appalling. It throws out these figures of millions of dollars, but what it is talking about in every case is the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. That is a security program. The farmer pays a premium just like an insurance policy and if he has a loss he receives a benefit. It is the same with crop insurance. The Government talks about crop insurance with great benevolence, but the crop insurance program is a program where the farmer pays a premium and if he has a loss he receives the benefit.
The Government talks about the western transportation Crow benefit. In fact, I am told that the full amount of the $659 million Crow benefit has not even been paid to the railroads. In fact, they are about $75 million short on the last two crop years. But the Government has made the payments for which it is legally obligated, otherwise it could be charged for not doing so. What the Government has done with the farm debt crisis is pretty bloody poor. What it is doing is providing some interest rate set aside on some farm loans for the FCC, but if the value of the commodity goes up, the farmer will end up actually paying more than the FCC rate, and if he does not have an FCC loan, he does not get anything.
The Minister promised a year ago last July 10 that he was going to bring in a Farm Debt Review Board with real clout and power. It took him 11 months to bring in anything, and then of course its fangs were totally pulled. The Government's action with regard to the tremendous farm crisis we face in this country is pretty puny when compared with what is being done in the United States, in the European Economic Community, or even what is being done by most provincial Governments. The Government has cut back on the budget of the Department of Agriculture by some $50 million and also it deindexed the annual rates within the Department. The Farm Credit Corporation in the 1984-85 fiscal year had a budget of $825 million. Last year it was something less than $250 million. There is not very much help beyond those statutory programs which the Government is obligated to provide.
Another problem has arisen with the United States Farm Bill and the countervail it put on hogs, and the BISEP program where the United States has tried to steal our markets in Egypt, Syria and other countries. The Prime Minister sang "When Irish Eyes are Smiling" in Quebec City and I think a lot of people assumed Ronny was going to look after us, that all the Prime Minister had to do was to give the President a call and it would all be straightened out. But all they have to do to learn the truth is to look at the two or three torpedoes which have gone through the "free enterprise battleship" in this last week. The Americans have ripped holes about two feet across below the waterline. That is the assistance and help we are receiving from the programs of the United States Government, which it is adopting around the world. There is certainly no exclusion for Canadian agriculture producers.
As I indicated when I began to speak, I only had a couple of brief comments to make. I want to indicate our support for Bill C-12 because I think, although some of these amendments are technical, they will be very beneficial for the individual producers. We want to assist the Minister in expediting the passage of Bill C-12.
