The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mayer that Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-12 is a Bill to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, which is an Act which has been around, as the Minister said, since 1956, 1957. It is an integral part of the legislation which rules the prairie grain industry. As most Hon. Members in the House know, prairie grain has been sold under the Canadian Wheat Board in one form or another since 1935. It became a compulsory board in 1942, I believe, and began using the quota system to regulate deliveries shortly after that.
The quota system was originally based on the amount of acres a farmer had. Over the years it has varied. At some time it was based on the amount of acres which was seeded to a particular grain. Then the summer fallow and grass acres were added to the quota base. Now we have a fairly sophisticated calculation of the quota base for each farm, and the farmer decides what proportion of each of the crops he is growing to allocate to that quota base.
I will go through the changes I see in this particular Bill in a few moments, but right now I would like to speak a wee bit about the role the cash advance system plays in prairie agriculture. Because of the system of forwarding grain through the quota system, there are occasionally times when producers are not called upon to deliver any grain, and if they cannot deliver any grain, they do not have any money. One of those times is with us at the moment. There was not even a quota opening until just a few days ago, which meant that producers had gone on for over two months without the ability to deliver any grain from this year's crop. In the interim, farm families must live, so back in the 1950s, under the then Minister, who is now the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), the Act was introduced which permitted farmers to take an advance on the grain they had in storage on their farms. This provided interim financing and in later years made it possible for the Wheat Board to be more careful about how it called its grain forward. It tries to practice a system whereby when orders are completed, sales are made, and ships are expected, some five to six weeks before the ship is expected to be at the dock, the quota for that particular grade and type of grain is opened up. The farmers deliver it to the elevators.
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
The elevator companies put it into the hopper cars which are transported by the railways to the terminals. The grain is cleaned and transloaded there and spouted into the waiting ship, usually with an amazing amount of efficiency and good timing when you consider all the people and active parties involved in the process.
I advise all Members of the House to consider paying an official call on the offices of the Canadian Wheat Board in order to watch its computer which shows the operations of the country's elevator and shipping system. Members will see how technicians in the Wheat Board keep track of where the grain is, how long it will be in transit, what ships are in need of loading, and so on. Such a visit will provide a better understanding of how the system operates. I recommend this visit not only to western Members but also to those who come from other parts of Canada.
The grain business in Canada is and always has been cyclical. It runs in cycles of seven to 10 years with a seven or eight-year down period and a seven or eight-year up period with some variations of a year or two either way. It is a cycle that Joseph noticed back in biblical days, and it has not changed a great deal in 2,000 or 3,000 years. Because of its cyclical nature the Canadian Government, at the urging of farmers and their organizations, has been actively involved in providing a certain number of protective mechanisms to help weather the inevitable storms. There is a tendency for production to build up in the world, which results in decreased demand and lowered prices. That is the type of situation we have seen in the last few years. A great deal of new technology has been applied in not only highly developed countries such as the European countries and the Americas but also in some developing countries such as China and India. In particular, China and India have succeeded in becoming self-sufficient in grains over the last number of years to the surprise of almost all the experts in the field. If any expert had looked at the productive capabilities of these two countries a few years ago I do not think it would have been predicted that China and India would be self-sufficient in the production of all grains today. In fact, they are now in the market-place as sellers of wheat and rice.
As a result, some countries have reacted in different ways. European countries have a long-standing program of agriculture subsidy which goes back to the fact that their citizens starved during the First and Second World Wars. The electorate remembers those days and therefore supports the type of system that has been put in place in which food imports are charged a high levy. The accumulated funds from these levies go to subsidize and encourage the production of the same food products in the European Economic Community. The system has worked almost too well. It has worked to the point where most of the food products produced inside the EEC are at or near a surplus level of production. This has resulted in fewer imports. Foreign exporters are no longer paying subsidies to keep the system running. The system is

being paid for almost exclusively out of the pockets of the European taxpayer.
To give Hon. Members an idea of what sort of subsidies are involved in these countries I would like to compare the subsidies received by European farmers with the subsidies that American and Canadian farmers receive. The Canadian Wheat Board estimates that Canada will subsidize wheat producers in the period 1986-87, which is the current crop year, by 85 cents per bushel. This subsidy includes the so-called Crow benefit which is given to the railways, as a result of which farmers are supposed to reap lower railway charges. It also includes the western grain stabilization pay-outs that will be made this crop year, as well as the federal Government contributions to crop insurance claims which western farmers might have in case of hail or frost. While Canadian farmers receive 85 cents per bushel of wheat in subsidies, the United States pays its farmers approximately S2.63 Canadian per bushel while the Europeans pay about $3.13 Canadian per bushel.
In terms of barley, the Canadian subsidy is 33 cents per bushel while the Americans subsidize their barley growers at the rate of $1.05 per bushel. The Europeans subsidize at a rate of $3.11 per bushel. I could give statistics with respect to subsidies paid in other countries, in particular Japan. However, subsidy levels in that country are large and so scary that Members would think that I was exaggerating. In Japan, the level of subsidy approaches $20 per bushel for some grains, notably rapeseed. The figures are almost beyond belief. As a result of this situation, various countries have been attempting to reduce amounts of production in a preliminary fashion. These are moves taken in preparation of talks concerning the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. World production of grain has far exceeded demand over the last several years. This is the first year it appears that output will be slightly lower, although only marginally, than what the demand is expected to be next year. In part, this reduction in crops has been due to weather, although the Americans had in place an acreage reduction program as a result of which they paid their farmers not to seed grain. The Europeans had no particular program to discourage production, but as a result of hot and dry weather production decreased. The Australians faced a combination of reduced acreage and bad weather, as did the Soviets. Thus the over-all grain crop will be slightly less than world demand for the first time in some six years.
In this period of time some very frightening things have happened in terms of income for Canadian farmers. I make this point because the advance system which we have is designed to offset, in part, some of this problem. Although the system does not perform the job perfectly, it provides some income when sales are hard to make at the farm level. If we compare gross income figures generated by Canadian crops during the time the surplus began to build up back in the 1982-83 crop year with the current crop year, we will see what lowered prices have done to Canadian farmers. This will allow us to see what the response by Canadian farmers has been,
given that we have very little in the way of subsidies to assist income.
This year, farmers on the Prairies are expected to produce what will probably be a record crop. They will produce somewhere in the neighbourhood of 52 million tonnes, one of the best crops that has ever been produced. In 1982-83, a crop of some 45.3 million tonnes was produced and that crop had an estimated value of $7.5 billion. This year, because prices were dropping, farmers tried for more output. This year, 52 million tonnes have been produced and that will have an estimated value of just over $6 billion. Fifteen per cent more crop has been produced on the Prairies, generating 18 per cent less in gross income. In terms of purchasing power from the larger crop, it will actually be down by 37 per cent from what it was in the 1982-83 crop year.
Financing for prairie farmers is crucial at the moment. Prairie farmers have compared the deficiency payments American farmers receive with those they receive and are trying to point out that Canadian farmers need the same kind of incomes as their American counterparts in order to remain competitive both technically and in the marketing sense as well. They have estimated that for wheat and barley grown on the Prairies, a deficiency payment of just about $2 billion would be required to keep them at the same income level as American farmers. Adding in the smaller crops like flax, rye and rapeseed, it would require an extra $1 billion in deficiency payments. A recent study, just made public this morning by a farm task force in Ontario which looked at income deficiency problems right across Canada, indicated that to meet the same level of income support as American farmers enjoy, Canadian farmers would need a deficiency payment in excess of $4 billion.
I put that on the record to show what is required. All we have before us at the moment is Bill C-12, a Bill which makes some minor changes to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. To some extent, it changes the administration of the Act, leaving some of the decisions with the Minister rather than with the entire Cabinet. The Governor in Council route has proven to be a rather slow, ponderous way of doing things. Sometimes farmers wait six, eight or even 10 weeks simply to receive the form that must be filled out in order to apply for a cash advance.
I might point out that these cash advances have a limit of $30,000 per customer so they do not constitute a huge loan. They are limited and are made available according to the type and grade of grain a farmer grows.
There will be a slight change regarding the grade of grain as well. Previously the grade was set at the same time as the forms were being produced. The amount of coverage will now be set out by the Minister and the Act itself will limit the coverage of the advance to two-thirds of the amount of the initial price for a grade of grain which the Minister may specify. The past practice has been for that to be based on No.
October 21, 1986

1 or No. 2 wheat or one feed barley. I assume that that will continue to be the practice, but we will have to find that out when the Minister comes before the legislative committee.
Through this Bill, the Minister announced some changes in the way defaults will be handled. We cannot be clear about what he has in mind from reading the Bill. Again, we will have to question him in committee.
The Minister is proposing to reduce the amount of interest payable by people who are in default. People who are in default are generally people who either misjudged or for some reason beyond their control were unable to deliver the amount of grain on which advances were taken. At times, there were no delivery opportunities for farmers to put grain into the elevator system so the advances were still outstanding at the end of the crop year.
As long as farmers have filled all the quotas that are available, the practice has been that they do not go into official default. However, if a grower does go into default during the year because he did not fill a quota that was opened on time and therefore missed the delivery opportunity, he is declared to be in default and is responsible for the interest payments at the rate established at the beginning of the year on the entirety of the advance, even if most of it has been paid off at the time of the default.
I hope that when the Minister speaks of taking the ability to deal with defaults into his own hands and the hands of the board, he is also speaking of some sort of clear direction as to how to handle these defaults. There are occasions when it has appeared as though things were not as fair as they might have been. A producer might have delivered 95 per cent of his crop but ended up defaulting at the very end with a mere 5 per cent still outstanding, but he will find that he is in fact by law responsible for paying interest on the whole of the cash advance for the whole period even though he had paid the greatest portion of it off before the default took place.
Through this Bill, the Minister is proposing changes to the method of deciding when advances should be made available for unthreshed grain. Again, rather than going to the Cabinet through the Governor in Council, the Minister will decide this, and that decision-making process should be much faster and less ponderous than has been the case. Likewise, as I understand the Bill, drying advances will now be initiated at the signature of the Minister rather than through the much slower process that I mentioned.
There are two other changes of which I wish to make mention. One of these changes is welcomed particularly by farmers who farm quite a bit of their own land but rent from one or several landlords, none of whom are contributing enough land to make up a very large per cent of the farmer's land base. The change proposed here is that rather than the current practice of being forced to go to every one of your landlords to get consent to apply for a $30,000 cash advance, you would be able to apply for a cash advance against your own grain, if you have more than $30,000 worth of grain on
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
your own account. You could take the loan against your own grain. In this manner you would not have to bother hunting up the landlords, some of whom are several thousand miles away, and getting their signatures, accompanied by those of the proper witnesses, which are very hard to come by.
The last change that is being proposed here is one that will need quite a bit of explanation from the Minister when we get into the committee. He is proposing to take the base for the cash advance from "acres" to "grain in storage". At first blush, I have no particular problem with that concept. I am wondering if there will be some administrative problems that may arise with this approach. In this Act the advances seem to be applicable to those grains that are coming under the Wheat Board. It is possible to collect advances on open market grain as they go through quotas. But there are some deliveries of off-board grain that do not go through quotas: Direct sales to neighbours, feed mills, and so on. There will be situations where grain trickles outside the system and the advances are not reclaimed. How is the Minister hoping to collect these and keep track of them, or is he foreseeing the same problems with the one system using a bushel base rather than an acreage base? Have his officials worked through the calculations to find out whether people who are farming acreages that, due to high production, would put them up to the maximum qualification of $30,000 worth of loan, would get enough quota during these rather clogged years for them to clean up the advance? What sort of administrative abilities are going to be provided at the end of that crop year to carry that grain on further? Does the Minister then propose to carry on a program mentioned by the Wheat Board several years ago whereby farmers who produced very high volumes of grain on their acreages could assign their grain and thus be guaranteed delivery of it by signing contracts such as are now being experimented with for one more year with regard to barley?
These amendments, while they do not change by one iota the financial situation that was alluded to at the beginning of my speech, they do make it a little simpler for farmers to get quick action from the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). These requirements mean that he will no longer be required to sit and wait for the due process to take place, to get the forms, the applications, and the current set of regulations through Cabinet each and every year. This process has caused farmers to wait until November and December in many years for their cash advance applications.
We applaud those small improvements to the system. We do not see any extra money. Farmers will still only be able to borrow $30,000. Perhaps the Minister has decided that this is prudent, given the declining values of grain in the world markets and the fact that he has found himself reducing the initial prices at the beginning of the crop year by $30 a tonne.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather historic that we are debating this cash advance legislation almost 29 years to the day after the
October 21, 1986

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
original Bill was passed. It has been mentioned by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). After the debate on the Speech from the Throne was over, the first item that came up was this cash advance legislation. It was in for one day, and the next day the old age security Bill was brought in and the amount was raised up to $55. Then we came back to this subject after that went through quickly.
The point I want to make today is not the matter of time, but the significance, not the significance to farmers, but to the people who serve the farmers, the merchants in the towns who are carrying the farmers all during the summer. This is a cash flow situation. I thought it would have been emphasized more by the Opposition, because these are the big beneficiaries of this. Why does the farmer like it? Because he likes sometimes to pay off his debts, particularly when they are to his friends in the town whom he depends on to service his equipment and provide him with all the other services. These communities in the rural areas of the Prairies are fighting a desperate battle to survive. This is very important legislation to them.
It would be wise for those in this House who are seriously interested in the reasons we brought in this legislation so quickly in 1957, to refer to Hansard of October 28, 1957, at page 477. You could read through the performances-and I remember them, of course, it was my maiden speech in the House-and follow a chap like the Right Hon. James Gardiner and a few others. On that Bill there were three names: Churchill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Harkness, the Minister of Agriculture; and my own name from Resources. The significance of that should not pass unnoticed. This was to help the whole national development picture, to get our agriculture moving and to take opportunities that then existed to spread our productive ability all over the world, instead of sitting around here and waiting for people to come and ask for it. That was the significance. You had to give to the farmer the cash flow, because under the system that we had, it was two years before he got full payment for that wheat. By speeding it up even to a partial extent, it allowed him to pay off a portion of his immediate debts. That is the economic significance of it. When you are writing your householder, ask the farmers out there to use it and to help their businessmen in the towns. The farmers will not be angry if you tell them. They know very well they should be doing this. Many of them in the south country-I know that is so in my constituency-do not take them. They look on that as something that is not a gift, it is their own money, and they get it deducted when they get payment. To many of the general people across the country when we talk about cash advances, when we talk about interim payment or initial payments on grains, when we talk about insurance, when we talk about stabilization, all these things are the farmers own money. This cleavage between the city people and the Province of Saskatchewan, at least, is disgraceful. The city people benefit in direct proportion, and double as much as the farmer, every time the farmer gets anything. If you want to revive the economy of any country, particularly the newly developing countries, you have to teach them that when you get wealth into the hands of the
producer, whether it be lumber, fish or agriculture, the city guy always benefits. This is how you bring peace to these countries, and it should bring peace to us in Saskatchewan. When you help the other person, you help yourself and both sides benefit. I think I have made my point right off the bat.
I was disappointed in the speech given by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). He knows a great deal about the details of these things. He should know that it is the duty of the Opposition to bring out these important points. He should know that you gain nothing with farmers by trying to go off at some other angle. His speech on the credibility of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) helps us. Politically it is helping us as Conservatives. People know that for many, many decades the political activities of members of the Liberal Party, whenever the Conservative Party got a leader, were not to talk about policies but to tear the leader down. I am not talking about just one or two of them, I am talking about one of the most positive persons that I have ever met in policy making, namely, the Hon. George Drew. He was torn apart even before he got into an election. He was called "the man from Bay Street", "the Colonel", and all the rest of it. He was torn apart by the press and torn apart by the Liberal Party, and they succeeded. You break a man down, you get rid of him. I would think that, with the positive thoughts I know the Hon. Member for Algoma has, he should not be trying to hurt his Party, because the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of this tactic.
It used to be that all politicians were down the drain pretty far, but in the last couple of years I can sense a change in the feelings of the people. They are angry at the media now. They are still mad at us, and we deserve it too, but the media is shooting out its brains the same way as the Member for Algoma was shooting out the brains of the Liberal Party today. I have to thank him because I know he helps us politically, as the farmers and the business people of rural Saskatchewan showed yesterday. Every Liberal candidate in that election lost his deposit, except for one. He is a local character and Leader of the Party. The people stood by him in his area and he deserved to win.
As politicians we have to do our job. When it is clear that what we are doing is hurting our Parliament and hurting our country, I would think that one should see the cloud on the horizon before it dumps on you. I am sorry to see the same type of tactics being used by certain people in the Liberal Party against their own Leader. No matter what you think of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), he is an Hon. Member of this House and deserves to be treated as such.
I have no excuse for all these people trying to make a million bucks writing books on themselves. It is bad enough when the media do it, but when politicians get into the act, that is the nth degree of low level living. I think I have said enough on that.
October 21, 1986

1 would suggest that if Hon. Members are interested in the basic problems facing the people of the Prairies in the period after the war, they should not only read my speech but read the debates of all the others as well. The Liberal Party and the NDP both supported this legislation and then spent most of the time in the House in that debate, as those who will read it will find out, trying to gut each other.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What has changed?

In those days members of the New Democratic Party were not pro Liberal, but they hurt themselves. I think the people of rural Canada are trying to tell politicians today to cut out this nonsense of making trivia of the main things that we talk about.
The number of things the Minister mentioned in his speech that have been done along this line show very rapid progress. I would think that the trouble may be that mistakes may be made by trying to go too fast. I think these things should be mentioned in good, constructive opposition. When you find something wrong that the Government has done, you let them have it.
1 will conclude my remarks by saying that this Bill we have before us is part of a much wider program that was announced by the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958. I will not read the whole speech but I will read points from the speech. Diefen-baker was the Prime Minister. I will summarize his speech in six points. First, I will read the introduction. It was a sound, comprehensive and co-ordinated program to attack specific problems. In developing a national agricultural policy we have found it necessary to deal with specific regional problems. He listed things about the West. I think any person in this House seriously interested in finding the basic philosophy, which still holds today, should read that speech of the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958. It can be found in Hansard at page 4345.
These points are: First, accelerated export sales. What a difference between 1957 and 1986. Twenty-nine years have gone by. They could not even sell the 300 million bushels we had for sale at that time. Second, stabilization of price and income policies. That is what this is, part of the stabilization of income. Third, assistance to provinces for recurring drought needs. Everybody in the House knows that for 30 years now we have kept our eye on any part of agriculture in any part of this country on any type of product. All Parties have come through on that. Fourth, a modern system of farm credit. I am not so proud of that because they got turned backwards on that one. On the modern system of farm credit, we put in by statutory rule that the ceiling on interest rates for farmers for long-term loans was 5 per cent. On the Farm Improvement Loan Act we put in a maximum of 6 per cent. I sat in this Parliament and watched those interest rates take off. What protest did we get? This measure went through quietly. It turned the poor farmer into the tender hands of the banks and the interest rates set by these people in Finance and in the Bank of Canada who are using interest rates to fight inflation, rising costs. Interest rates were the inflation. Those dimwits who still pollute those offices
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
are still at it. They are begrudgingly coming down. This Parliament in 1983, all the Parties, gave to the Government of the day the power to move on housing, agriculture, small business, and we sit here today knowing the Government has made an effort but it has not succeeded on the fiscal side because it forgot to read its own regulations. That is what Members of Parliament are here for. We have to read the small print. You can only lend money under this program to people in dire straits. That is still there.
The Government changed in 1984, so if you are talking about this general program of helping farmers, a good Opposition would be pointing out these things. Why do you have to leave it to a Member on this side of the House to do it? Come on, fellows, get the finger out or you are going to choke yourselves to death.
The final point concerns national conservation programs which are mainly concerned with clean water and clean air. Tremendous progress has been made in the last 30 years on the scientific and practical side. However, no Party in this House will ever tell you what these practical things are. The work we started in the 1950s was announced in this House in 1973 by a Liberal Minister. He was very proud that this revolutionary step forward had been taken concerning clean water. Revolutionary, he said, and it was. Two years later I asked the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Hon. Don MacDonald, who I knew read everything, is it not about time that he told Canada about operation CANWELL? Civil servants and scientists have worked hard in Ontario and Quebec to develop these techniques and make money out of cleaning up the air and water. What was his answer? "You tell them, not me". I am still trying to get it across. In that respect we have a lot to do, but if we use the philosophy in this legislation and apply it to all other types of legislation, then agriculture, including all the producing groups, is the main beneficiary.
This legislation is technical, it is true. The points made by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Alt-house) are good. He missed the main point, that the revolutionary thing in this legislation is that you have taken the power out of the hands of Ottawa civil servants and put it in the hands of the Wheat Board. Ye gods, if you knew the time a Minister has to take to get something through in this system! It is good legislation, but try and see it in perspective. Try to see it for what it can do if we apply this reasoning to a lot of other things we have before us.
I am very proud to be able to stand up 29 years later and say I was responsible for drafting it, which is true. Do not blame the Liberals or the NDP for the time it takes. Poor Mr. Gardiner tried his level best to put the blame on Mr. Howe, his good friend. Really it was not Howe's fault or Gardiner's fault. The civil servants had decided it was not possible to do this kind of practical thing. I do not blame those people for getting up and trying to shift the blame, but the point I am trying to

October 21, 1986
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
leave with Members of Parliament is that when you have practical, technical legislation like this going through, look into the background so you can see the future. We have to do this not only for grain farmers but for many forms of basic production. We have to have a stabilized income and stabilized costs. Move slowly but stabilize it.
I did not have time to say all the things I intended, but I think my point has been made. The philosophy of John Diefenbaker lives still. When we honoured him with that statue out there I had a feeling he was going to keep an eye on us here. I suspect a lot of us still feel his presence. The great things he did were never matched by all the Governments put together since Confederation, by quantitative analysis, and they should not just be remembered in a statue unveiling. They should be part of our actions.
I congratulate the Minister for bringing this forward and I hope there is a lot more coming from other Ministers as well.
Mir. Deputy Speaker: Questions and comments?

Mr. Speaker, I must say it has been a pleasure to listen for the last 20 minutes to the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). He has an honourable place in the development of economic policy in Canada and in the history of the Diefenbaker Government between 1957 and 1963. I must say, having practised as a Canadian historian, that I have been awaiting a speech by him and I am so very pleased I was in the House this afternoon to hear him speak.
The fact that he spoke broadly on a variety of things, some of them very interesting indeed, encourages me to wonder whether I might ask a question which takes us a bit beyond the Bill before us this afternoon, although I do not think it is unrelated. The Diefenbaker years were years of economic initiatives of enormous importance to prairie farmers, the prairie population generally, and to Atlantic Canada. Unfortunately, they ended up being years of very significant deficits as well. Perhaps this was a result of economic policy contradictions at the time. These days we face high deficits again, and this is the primary problem which the Government of the day seems to be concerned about. We certainly have not seen in these last days that kind of sharp and ready response to the needs of prairie farmers which I think characterized the Diefenbaker Government, as the hon. gentleman pointed out to us.
I wonder whether, in the contradictions between the Bank of Canada and the then Minister of Finance, and the Hon. Member's efforts as a Minister to put in place national development policies which would make Canada a better and richer country than it was when the Government he was part of took office, he would have any advice for us in our circumstances in the 1980s about how we might develop the country and get beyond the deficits which the Government finds so encumbering.

until we get this thing going. The economy is rising by two or three points a year. If we let it speed up for another couple of years we will pull out. We must make legislation to stop adding to programs which are non-remunerative.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for a very good answer. The concern he mentioned about the circumstances being different today reminded me of the arguments I have read about which R. B. Bennett made. He waited a little too long. Is it not possible, in circumstances which seem different, to do the things of which the Member spoke? Would it not be better to do them in 1986 than to wait and go down to defeat in 1989?

Mr. Speaker, I think the answer is the same. If you are on a little raft and want to jump a long distance, you try to get more support around the raft before you jump. There is a point at which it is silly to talk about spending money to make money, (a) when you do not have it and, and (b) when you do not have the foundation from which to leap off. We did not have that situation from 1957 to 1959 because we had a pretty good period in the early 1950s. Money had flowed into this country like mad forcing our dollar up to around $1.07. We had to face all these problems.
The experts were advising restraint and paying our way slowly out of these difficulties. We had enough base to jump ahead on a few small things. We could take wheat sales to 10 communist countries rather than just one. We broke out and never lost a cent in the whole deal. All the banks were worrying that we would never repay them. The solution was to help them sell their goods in order to get enough money to pay for it. That is why I support freer trade. That is what I call my "peace through trade" policies.
I am in contact with 86 countries. They ask what they can do to make some money. I tell them what they can do. We do not give them money. They do not really want it. If you can show them ways in which to earn it themselves it is much better. The positive approach has weaknesses, of course, but the fact is that you must have that base. We are accumulating that base pretty effectively right now and it is about time to move.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to break in on this philosophical approach to the deficit, but I do want to say a few words on this Bill. If the Government agrees, I suggest that this Bill could be referred to committee at the end of this sitting. Many of the factors which led to the crisis in agriculture in Canada are still in place. I refer, of course, to things like the high interest rates in the 1970s and early 1980s, the declining value of farm assets and the annually rising costs of farm inputs such as fuel, fertilizer and chemicals. Perhaps the most important entity is the continuing decline of commodity prices. All of those factors have contributed to the current crisis in agriculture.
It is unclear whether the decline in agricultural income has bottomed out. We are not at all sure that the small rise which
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
we have experienced in the prices of red meats and pork is going to continue. We do not even know whether the price of grain will continue to decline. I applaud the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) for putting in place a Bill which will allow cash advances for harvested grain to be more easily and readily available without the problems faced by farmers and the Wheat Board over the years. Consequently, we will be supporting this Bill. I suggest that it could go to the committee at the end of today's sitting.
Farmers face cash flow problems at almost any time. Most people who do not live in farming communities do not realize that it takes approximately two years before the farmer realizes a return on his initial investment. The farmer will buy the fertilizer, seed and other material in the fall but will not bring off the crop until two years later. He may still be selling the crop two years later. That is a long time for any business person to wait for a return, and if the business is declining and cash flow is small it is important that parliamentarians and the Government provide some relief and have a return in eight months rather than two years.
Bill C-12 is a worth-while effort to improve that relief process and we are pleased that the Minister has brought it forward. When the Bill goes to committee, we will question the Minister on a number of aspects that should be considered, not only in the Bill itself, but in the regulations attached to it. Cash advances are not the solution to the problem, as I know the Government recognizes. It is a band-aid solution to some extent, and farmers would be pleased to get along without cash advances. A much more global approach is needed to address the problems of agriculture.
There is a widespread concern within the agricultural community that the Government believes that one of the solutions to the problem facing farming is to have fewer farmers. The Government has contributed to this concern to some extent, as a result of doing what it believes is helpful to the farmer. The agricultural community sees the Government carrying out programs that may be beneficial but which also indicate that perhaps the Government is not interested in finding a total solution that will keep farmers farming for many years. It is important that we keep reminding the Government about this fear.
The Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) fuzzy approach in announcing a billion dollars in assistance for grain farmers has confused the farm community rather than provided it with some security. For example, we are not sure how much the assistance will be, how it will be paid, how much will be paid, or how it will be financed. We do not even know who is eligible for these payments.
The terms of this assistance are so nebulous that it is very difficult to know exactly how it will work. The farmers cannot say with certainty that they have an agreement by which they will get a certain price for their grain or a certain amount in assistance that they need. Consequently, the Government must

October 21, 1986
Adjournment Debate
develop in the next two years a global approach that will not include band-aid solutions. Although it is difficult to suggest that $1 billion in assistance is a band-aid solution, that is what it amounts to.
While the changes proposed in the Bill are beneficial, a number of the Wheat Board's and Ministers' responsibilities are not spelled out in the Bill. The present Act and the changes in the Bill do not clearly specify that inflexibility will not appear in the new structure so that farmers will still find themselves acquiring debts they should not have acquired because of the way in which the Act has been interpreted and used to collect money from the farmers. We will be discussing this area very thoroughly in the committee.
However, the changes in the Bill are worthwhile and I hope the Bill will receive speedy passage.

Mr. Speaker, first, may I take this opportunity to congratulate you on your reappointment to the chair. You did an excellent job in the previous session, as I am sure you will do this year.
I also want to commend the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle- Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I do not think there is any time when the Hon. Member speaks that we do not enjoy listening to him because he has such a tremendous knowledge of the past. I recall the years when he was the Minister of Agriculture, when our granaries were jammed with wheat and we had no place to send it. The Hon. Member went to China and came back with an order that took a large volume of that wheat. He has a tremendous record and I want to thank him for what he has done for Canada and for agriculture.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-SEWAGE TREATMENT FACILITIES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-SEWAGE TREATMENT FACILITIES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a question I put to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) on October 7 concerning the Governmment's inadequate funding of sewage treatment plants.
When I asked the Minister why, in spite of the grandiloquent rhetoric of the Speech from the Throne on environmental issues, he turned down requests from provincial Ministers
for additional federal funds for building new and upgrading existing sewage treatment plants, he answered that the Government was already "up to its eyebrows" in such funding. But, when boasting about his Government's record, the Minister did not mention that the tens of millions of dollars he has committed to the provinces are actually small potatoes beside the $1.8 billion in loans and grants provided to the provinces for sewage treatment facilities through CMHC programs in the period from 1961 through 1980.
Nor did the Minister mention that of the $65 million he bragged about giving to Ontario, a mere $9.7 million remains available, and this was as a result of an agreement which may well go back to 1980, prior to the election of the Conservative Government.
The consequences of the Government's environmental irresponsiblity through continuing inaction are indeed grave. According to last year's federal inquiry into water policy, a disgraceful 43 per cent of Canada is not served by any form of sewage treatment facilities. Even where there are plants in operation, they are often inadequate to the task, causing leakages and overflows of raw sewage into Canadian waters. The almost annual closure of beaches in the St. Catharines region is a direct result of inadequate sewage facilities causing overflows.
The underfunding of sewage treatment plants is only one of many areas where the Government's failure to live up to its environmental responsibilities has led to the dangerous deterioration of Canada's water supplies. Be it sewage treatment, toxic wastes being dumped deliberately into our waters or pesticides draining off fields into our lakes and rivers, the Government so far has not been up to the challenge.

A tragic example of this lack of responsibility, Mr. Speaker, is the case of white whales in the St. Lawrence River. One hundred years ago there were 5,000 white whales in the St. Lawrence River; fifty years later there were only half as many as a result of commercial hunting. Today only 400 whales ply these waters, and pollution rather than hunters is the enemy.
Biologists who examine white whales which often beach themselves on the shores of the St. Lawrence River have been able to determine that their bodies contain all kinds of toxins, including PCBs. Where do these poisons come from? From Jonquiere's Alcan plant, right next to the whale's habitat. They also come from pesticides dumped into the St. Lawrence, and they come from raw sewage.
When we hear about the problem of toxic chemicals in Canadian waters, invariably reference is made to the Great Lakes, the Niagara River and the St. Clair River. The sad story of white whales in the St. Lawrence River clearly indicates that the Government must also tackle the serious problem of polluted waters in the St. Lawrence River.
October 21, 1986



Greenpeace, which is currently campaigning to save the beluga whale, estimates that the beluga will be extinct in its St. Lawrence habitat by the year 2000. Urgent action is needed if we are to avert this tragedy. However, urgent action is never what we seem to get from the Government. Its response to the sewage treatment problem, "Look what we've done in the past", is all too typical of the Minister's response to environmental problems. He has been extremely light on action so far despite the great expectations which greeted his appointment as Minister of the Environment. He is very big on words which are full of sound and fury but signify nothing. We hope at some point that "nothing" will turn into something, and with respect to the St. Lawrence River, the Niagara River problem, acid rain, pesticides, and so many of the serious environmental problems facing this country, we will see action forthcoming from the Government.
I look forward to hearing just what type of action the Government has in mind from whoever has been designated to respond on behalf of the Minister. Perhaps this will be an occasion on which we will hear something new from the Government, something about which I can only hope.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-SEWAGE TREATMENT FACILITIES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to have an opportunity to reply to the Hon. Member's question about possible federal funding for the upgrading of municipal infrastructure facilities.
As Members of the House are aware, on October 2, 1986, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) met with his provincial counterparts at the annual meeting of the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. During the frank and constructive discussion, the federal and provincial Environment Ministers agreed that the need for new and upgraded municipal and sewer waterworks is an issue of growing significance which will have to be addressed by all three levels of Government. The Ministers also agreed that the responsibility extends well beyond the mandate of Environment and Resource Ministers and must be addressed by First Ministers and Ministers of Finance.
To date, the debate has focused exclusively on the question of potential financing by federal and provincial Governments. While the financing question is important, it is the view of the federal and provincial Ministers that appropriate pricing of water services is the other side of the same coin and that appropriate pricing must be considered on a priority basis in parallel with the issue of subsidies. Canadians must look at the potential benefits of applying the user-pay principle to the provision of water supply and waste water treatment services to a greater degree than is currently being done.
In this regard the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers agreed to establish an advisory committee on water. The first task of this committee will be to
Adjournment Debate
oversee a study on the cost of delivering and treating water as one aspect of the fiscal dimension of the problem. We must also take into account other important considerations. Collectively, Canadians must search for new solutions. For example, Environment Canada officials are examining the potential for improved efficiencies in sewage treatment through technological innovation, and the Department of Health and Welfare is pursuing similar initiatives in relation to drinking water.
In addition to any study of methods to finance the upgrading of municipal infrastructure, the federal Government has signed with the various provinces a number of economic and regional development agreements respecting municipal infrastructure. The agreements cover matters such as provision of water supply, sewer and waste water treatment systems, as well as provision of drainage systems to assist with community and industrial development.
The problem is being addressed, and Canada is up to the challenge.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENT FOR FARMERS. (B) SITUATION OF GRAIN FARMERS
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENT FOR FARMERS. (B) SITUATION OF GRAIN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 3 I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) if the Government would provide a deficiency payment to Canadian grain producers who are facing the worst prices for grain since the 1930s. The Minister declined to respond to my question. I also pointed out that a few weeks ago the Government was able to find some $1.5 billion for the major 25 oil companies, most of them multinationals. I asked why the Government could find no assistance for the 140 grain farmers in western Canada, as well as the other grain farmers producing in Ontario and other provinces, as well as corn producers.
On the previous day, the Regina Leader-Post had pointed out how the Speech from the Throne had mentioned in only very general terms what the Government would do. An article which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post on October 2 reads as follows:
The lack of detail on agriculture must be a particular concern in this province. True, agriculture rated mention near the beginning of the speech-not long after Sauve told us what she did this summer.
Prairie grain farmers know what they did this summer: they produced a record crop-
Many Saskatchewan ears therefore were tuned to hear whether a deficiency payment would be forthcoming from Ottawa.
About the time this comment appeared in an editorial in the Regina Leader-Post, there was a frantic phone call from Premier Grant Devine of Saskatchewan, supposedly to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) at 5.30 in the morning. As heard by a reporter, the Premier was demanding that the Government announce a deficiency payment.

October 21, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The same day I asked my question, even though the Minister of Agriculture gave his usual blather containing no answer to my question, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), responding to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, made this statement to the House:
I am pleased to announce today that we will be working closely over the next month with Premier Devine and other provincial Governments to devise an effective financial assistance program to enhance the cash flow of Canadian grain farmers. Initial estimates of the assistance required are that it will amount to approximately $1 billion.
That was very skillfully worded. He did not say anything about a deficiency payment. He did not say the Government would give $1 billion. He just said that there is a need for $1 billion. Everyone is aware that there is a need for probably $2 billion or S3 billion rather than the amount about which the Government is speaking.
During the Question Period of Monday, October 6, in reply to a question put by the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister said that the Government must move forward with aid for farmers and made the comment that it must produce the information required to help western farmers. On the same day during Question Period, he talked about taking whatever action would be helpful to western farmers.
Outside the House that day, the Minister of Agriculture suddenly waded into the question and announced that actually the $1 billion would not just go to western grain farmers. In other words, if $2 billion was required across the country, only $.5 billion would go to western farmers. He was very careful not to say how much would be provided for western farmers. As a matter of fact, he did volunteer that the Atlantic Feed Grain Initiative Program might be increased from $30 million to $50 million, at least according to a press report.
According to another article of October 8, the Minister said that the aid might not be a deficiency payment, it might be a loan guarantee or it might be some other loan program. This was especially disturbing to farmers across Canada because most of them already have too much debt. They do not want any more loans. They do not want loan guarantees. They want a deficiency payment.
The Parliamentary Secretary who will be responding today represents an agricultural area which is facing difficult times. The tobacco farmers of southwestern Ontario are facing as difficult times as are the grain farmers and corn producers in southwestern Ontario and the grain farmers in western Canada. I hope that he will muster up his courage, stop the flim-flam, the obfuscations, the double-talk, and stop the headline hunting and reaching for the headlines, as the Prime Minister does all the time, but not reaching for the Government's pocket-book.
We have a very serious problem in agriculture today. The Government has known about this problem since it announced the initial price for wheat last April or May. Now is the time
for the Parliamentary Secretary to come clean and announce what the terms and conditions will be; whether it will be a deficiency payment, how it will be paid and what amount for each region of the country. The Government can stop this situation of Canadians not knowing what is going to happen to our most important and vital industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENT FOR FARMERS. (B) SITUATION OF GRAIN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour this evening to represent someone who has done so much in the last two years for farmers and has achieved so much for that same group of people, much more than anyone else for many a moon.
Since the question from the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) was first raised in the House, several steps have been taken to build on this Government's commitment to Canadian farmers. We have left no doubt about our intention to extend financial assistance to grain farmers who have become victims of the subsidy war between western Europe and the United States. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been highly supportive of Canadian agriculture from day one of this Government. He once again demonstrated his commitment to our farmers on October 3 when he announced to this House that the federal Government will work with provincial governments to enhance the cash flow of Canadian grain farmers. Initial estimates of the assistance required are in the neighbourhood of $1 billion.
How can we make the assistance equitable? What kind of assistance package will do the most good? These are the questions we must answer. It is a national problem. The solution must also be national. It must be fair and it must be equitable.
That is why we are consulting with farm organizations and acting in concert with the provinces. Together, we will come up with a package that puts money into the hands of Canadian farmers as soon as possible, but also as effectively as possible.
Federal and provincial Governments have been working together for some time to find ways of assisting Canadian grain farmers. At a meeting in Victoria on August 27, the federal and provincial Ministers of Agriculture made a collective commitment to take action to support the agricultural sector and all the jobs it represents across Canada. On October 9 federal and provincial Deputy Ministers of Agriculture once again met in Ottawa to continue the work of defining an assistance package. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) met with farm leaders on October 16. All options are being examined. Assistance could take many forms, from enhancing the existing programs to developing new initiatives.
Three points are clear. First, we are talking about assistance beyond funds available under existing programs. Second, any assistance will be within the federal Government's fiscal framework. Third, no federal program of agriculture will be cut in order to Finance this one.
October 21, 1986

The need for assistance is clear. This Government's commitment to take action is also clear. We intend to consult, then we intend to act fairly, equitably, and quickly.

Mr. Speaker, I know that you had a very busy and active summer. It would not surprise me at all if you did not have an opportunity to notice that in August the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police met in Winnipeg and passed some very important resolutions. I would like to bring on to your attention in the event that you did not have an opportunity to see it at the time. That resolution deals with firearms and gun control. It reads as follows:
WHEREAS the presence of restricted weapons particularly handguns in Canada is a concern to the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, and
WHEREAS the National Firearms Registry reports the annual average of firsttime registration of these weapons is in excess of 30,000, and
WHEREAS there is presently a world-wide surplus of automatic and semiautomatic weapons primarily designed for purposes of warfare now finding their way into the Canadian market-place, and-
WHEREAS Canadian public opinion is critical of the American handgun experience, and
WHEREAS present gun control laws are in need of review;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Solicitor General of Canada now address these concerns in conjunction with his provincial counterparts and take the steps necessary to end this increase in available weapons.
I know that even if you missed hearing that resolution firsthand, Mr. Speaker, you were present in this House and you did hear me question the then Minister of Justice on the subject of gun control back in February of this year. You heard the then Minister of Justice indicate to me at that time that he was reviewing gun control policy. You also heard, and I am sure that you read in the papers in May of this year, of a report by one counsel from the Department of Justice, Mr. Michael Zigayer, who indicated that there would be gun control amendments to the Criminal Code ready for introduction in legislation this fall. Again, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, on October 14, 1986 that I asked the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) what was happening with this gun control legislation and amendments. He indicated that the matter was still under review.
It is now the fall and it is time for action. Canadians are looking to the Government to introduce amendments to the gun control legislation. It will not be easy to come up with amendments that satisfy everybody. I believe, as I am sure you do, Mr. Speaker, that by and large the vast majority of urban dwellers in Canada feel that there should be stricter gun control laws. There are exceptions, of course, in the target shooters, the hunters, and also a large number of rural dwellers and some experts who feel that our gun control laws are too strict now. Regardless, we have to address this problem. When we do, and I hope it will be very soon, I hope that the Department of Justice will take into account the recommendations made by the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department for
Adjournment Debate
amendments to the Criminal Code in this respect. These suggestions flow from the concern of the Metro Police relating to the fact that in 1985 in Toronto there were some 512 occurrences of bullets being discharged, resulting in 16 deaths.
There is a concern as well relating to the growing numbers of military firearms, fully automatic and semi-automatic weapons. I would like to summarize some of the recommendations. The Toronto Police Department recommends, first, that the definition of a prohibited weapon be changed to include "any firearm that is designed, altered or intended to fire bullets in rapid succession by any means other than a single shot for each movement of the trigger by a finger. Any device that is designed or intended to enable a firearm to fire bullets in rapid succession other than a single shot for each movement of the trigger by a finger".
Second, they would like to see the definition of a restricted weapon changed to include "any military surplus or military designed semi-automatic or single shot firearm, or a weapon of any kind, not being a prohibited weapon, that is declared by order of the Governor in Council to be a restricted weapon". That would include "any device, chamber, clip or magazine that allows temporary or permanent access to more than 10 rounds of ammunition to any firearm without physically reloading the firearm".
Third, they would like to see the Criminal Code amended "to require any recipient of ammunition to produce a valid Firearms Acquisition Certificate to the person distributing the ammunition". Fourth, they would like to see that peace officers have "the authority to seize a Firearms Acquisition Certificate." Finally, they would like to see the Criminal Code amended so that any person who is authorized to issue a Firearms Acquisition Certification would also have authority to revoke it.
Those are the recommendations of the Metropolitan Toronto Police with respect to amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with firearms and gun control. I firmly believe that they should be taken very seriously by the Department of Justice. They should be taken into account when considering the forthcoming amendments. I hope we will hear from the Parliamentary Secretary that that is happening and that we are going to have some further amendments to the Criminal Code with respect to gun control very shortly, I trust before Christmas. When I say that, I mean before Christmas, 1986.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for his question, since it gives me an opportunity to provide a brief overview of our firearms legislation. First of all, I must point out that our Constitution, unlike that in the United States, does not recognize the right of citizens to carry arms. And in fact, the provisions of the U.S. Constitution that are interpreted as conferring such a right are not perfectly clear. In Canada, federal and provincial legislation authorizes the

October 21, 1986
Adjournment Debate
possession of firearms for legitimate activities such as target shooting, maintaining a collection and hunting, while prohibiting or strictly regulating possession in other cases.
The present provisions of the Criminal Code relating to firearms were introduced by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1977 (Bill C-51). The passage of this legislation was accompanied by lively debate both in the House and the Senate. Hunters and collectors maintained that the provisions in question would constitute an obstacle to legitimate activities, but would not prevent criminals from procuring firearms. Proponents of stricter regulations maintained, however, that the provisions did not go far enough.
The present regulations have therefore been in existence for nine years. While admittedly, the legislation has had a fairly satisfactory impact and is well received by Canadians, it would seem necessary to make some changes in the provisions introduced in 1977. These provisions have, in fact, given rise to a number of problems the legislators had not foreseen.
As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) stated in this House October 14 last, in answer to a question from the Hon.
Member for York East, the Government has launched a review of Criminal Code provisions concerning firearms. The idea is to draft amendment which, without flying in the face of the principles underlying the legislation on firearms, would clear up certain points of the law to make enforcement easier. One of the objectives is to give people better protection by improving some of the legislative provisions. Another objective is to change certain provisions which cause problems to those who own firearms for legitimate purposes but still do not contribute to protecting the public.
As the Minister of Justice pointed out, he hopes the recommendations on this issue will be submitted in the near future, and this will eventually lead to the introduction of legislative measures in this House. We are pleased to note the representations of the Hon. Member for York East.
